algorithm can work well with the unstable submarine transmission environment,
the non-ideal DFE learning process, and the higher order CD. Hence, the joint
WDFE and MLSE algorithm can be a reliable digital signal processing scheme for

handling inconsistencies in tables
with missing values (also called nulls) and functional dependencies. Although
the traditional view is that table instances must respect all functional
dependencies imposed on them, it is nevertheless relevant to develop theories
about how to handle instances that violate some dependencies. Regarding missing
values, we make no assumptions on their existence: a missing value exists only
if it is inferred from the functional dependencies of the table.
  We propose a formal framework in which each tuple of a table is associated
with a truth value among the following: true, false, inconsistent or unknown;
and we show that our framework can be used to study important problems such as
consistent query answering, table merging, and data quality measures - to
mention just a few. In this paper, however, we focus mainly on consistent query
answering, a problem that has received considerable attention during the last
decades.
  The main contributions of the paper are the following: (a) we introduce a new
approach to handle inconsistencies in a table with nulls and functional
dependencies, (b) we give algorithms for computing all true, inconsistent and
false tuples, (c) we investigate the relationship between our approach and
Four-valued logic in the context of data merging, and (d) we give a novel
solution to the consistent query answering problem and compare our solution to
that of table repairs.
  We believe that our frameworks and techniques can be used to study other
theoretical problems and, most importantly, they can be used to develop practical
algorithms for maintaining the data quality of tables with functional
dependencies.
  Keywords: Functional dependencies, missing values, data merging, data
quality, consistent query answering.

convolutional neural network (CNN) has received considerable attention.
Depending on whether intermediate cues are used, the relevant literature can be
roughly divided into two broad categories: direct methods and two stage
pipelines. For the latter, intermediate cues, such as 3D object coordinates,
semantic keypoints, or virtual control points instead of pose parameters are
regressed by CNN in the first stage. Object pose can then be solved by
correspondence constraints constructed with the regressed intermediate cues.
Both direct and two-stage pipelines have been proved to be effective for object
pose estimation. However, intermediate cues regressed by CNN are still
object-dependent, which means they may work for some objects but not work at all
for others due to the limited generalization ability of deep neural networks.
In this paper, we propose a novel framework which uses a single stage CNN to
solve the object pose estimation problem directly. Instead of object-dependent
intermediate cues, we propose to use a set of generic control points to
represent the 6D pose of any object instance. A robust and efficient pose
correspondence constraint construction strategy is further developed to match
the generic control points with the 3D object mesh. Extensive experiments on
three public datasets demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms all the
state-of-the-art methods in terms of accuracy and generalization ability.
Moreover, our method is also able to handle novel objects with a few images by
exploiting cross-dataset learning techniques, which is also unprecedented in
existing works on object pose estimation.

internal reflections within the lenses. In this work we investigated this issue
proposing a new lens material Stycast 1090SI. We characterized the acoustic
properties of the proposed material in comparison with PMMA. Detector
performance using negative lenses with the two materials, was tested using
finite element simulation and experiment. Further the image quality of a
photoacoustic tomography system was studied using k-Wave simulation and
experiment. Our acoustic characterization showed that Stycast 1090SI has
tissue-like acoustic impedance, high speed of sound and low acoustic
attenuation. Both acoustic lenses show significant enlargement of detector
acceptance angle and lateral resolution improvement. However, image artifacts
induced by acoustic lenses are reduced using the proposed lens compared to PMMA
lens.

artifacts without compromising lateral resolution. Such lenses can be promising
tools to improve detection sensitivity and image quality in photoacoustic and

be improved by simply increasing the diameter of the acoustic lens used in the
photoacoustic tomography system.

photoacoustic tomography image quality before experimentally validating the
design.

systems before experimentally validating them.

innovations.

design before building a prototype.

evaluate,and optimize a photoacoustic tomography system before experimentally
validating the design.

improving photoacoustic tomography systems and may lead to better patient
outcomes.

quantum gravity. By investigating large classes of Type IIB four-dimensional
$\mathcal{N}=2$ effective field theories, we enlist the potential generalized
global symmetries that could be present and explore how they are avoided.
Crucial ingredients that arise in such effective field theories are generalized
$\theta$-terms. These introduce non-linear couplings between axion fields and
topological terms quadratic in the gauge field strengths which break a large
subset of the global symmetries. Additional residual global symmetries may
further be broken by assuming the existence of some charged states. However, we
illustrate that the presence of generalized $\theta$-terms leads to a
generalized Witten effect, which implies that the spectrum of charged states is
constituted by an infinitely populated lattice. We further show that such a
lattice is generated by the action of the monodromy transformation that
characterizes the moduli space boundary near which the effective theory is
defined.
  Finally, we discuss the implications of these results for four-dimensional
$\mathcal{N}=2$ effective field theories that arise from compactifications of
Type IIB supergravity on six-dimensional manifolds with a boundary.
Generalized $\theta$-terms may be present in the absence of D7-branes. When
present, the global symmetries of the effective field theory are significantly
restricted. In particular, only the U(1)$_R$ symmetry is allowed to exist. If
no such symmetry is present, the compactification radius is forced to be of the
order-of-unit size, i.e. $R \sim 1$. Such a value of the radius leads to a
four-dimensional theory that is essentially five-dimensional Type IIB theory.
Finally, we note that the presence of certain non-perturbative effects, which
are expected to appear in Type IIB axiodilaton systems, should be considered a
must for the avoidance of global symmetries.
  This work is motivated from the investigation of the consistency of certain
four-dimensional $\mathcal{N}=2$ effective field theories that were obtained
from compactifications of Type IIB theory on manifolds with additional
geometry. Such consistency requires the absence of global symmetries in the
effective field theory. In a series of works we showed that this is generally
achieved provided that the axiodilaton coupling is strongly coupled.

minimizing the required trust for sandboxing malicious programs, provided that
security-critical programs are written to use the hardware correctly.

devices that are being used to study multi-phonon phenomena both theoretically

semiconductor quantum dot pumped by a driving laser, and coupled to an acoustic
cavity. This kind of systems has proven to yield interesting multi-phonon
phenomena, but the description of the quantum dot has been limited to a
two-level system. This limitation restrains the complexity that a true
semiconductor quantum dot can offer. Instead, in this work we consider a model
where the quantum dot can have both bright and dark excitons, the latter being
particularly useful due to their lower decoherence rates, because they do not
present spontaneous photon emission. In this setup, we demonstrate that by
fine-tuning the driving laser frequency, one is able to realise giant Rabi
oscillations between the vacuum state of the acoustic cavity and a multi-phonon
state with $2N$ phonons. This is considered a true multi-phonon phenomenon
because it is not possible to explain the observed oscillations through the
action of a single Rabi oscillation between two phonon states. We have found
that the generation of these giant oscillations is possible due to a
non-linear coupling between the quantum dot and the acoustic cavity, which
assists in the transfer of excitons from the quantum dot to the acoustic
cavity in large multiples. Additionally, we have demonstrated that this process
is able to be controlled by the laser driving frequency and detuning, as well

have found that this phenomenon is able to withstand considerable sources of

generation of multiple phonons in acoustic cavities.

  I. Introduction
  Chemical informatics is a subfield of informatics that deals with the
application of informatics to chemistry. One of the main research areas in
chemical informatics is drug design, which has been around for a few decades.
With the recent advancements in artificial neural networks (ANNs) and mixed
integer linear programming (MILP), there is a growing interest in designing the
molecular structure of chemical compounds with a desired chemical property.
Research along this line has been recently surveyed [1] and a framework for
inferring chemical compounds has been proposed [2, 3]. In brief, the framework
takes a set of chemical properties together with a set of possible atomic
components and a set of possible chemical bonds as input and outputs a
macro-molecule with the desired properties through a sequence of two steps.
First, a prediction function constructed from a type of machine learning
algorithm predicts a set of descriptors from the input data; second, a
constraint-programming method is used to find a molecular structure from the
predicted descriptors and the given input data. With the framework, we can
design chemical compounds, infer polymers from monomers, and even discover new
chemical properties. In this paper, we focus on inferring a polymer from a
monomer and, to this end, we construct a prediction function from linear
regression, a simple machine learning algorithm, as a building block of the
framework.

to be very challenging. This is due to the low contrast between the tumor and
adjacent tissues, the anatomical variation of the esophagus, as well as the
occasional presence of foreign bodies (e.g. feeding tubes). Physicians
therefore usually exploit additional knowledge such as endoscopic findings,
clinical history, additional imaging modalities (e.g. PET scans). Achieving his
additional information is time-consuming, while the results are error-prone and
might lead to non-deterministic results. In this paper we aim to investigate if
and to what extent a simplified clinical workflow based on CT alone, allows one
to automatically segment the esophageal tumor with sufficient quality. For this
purpose, we present a fully automatic end-to-end esophageal tumor segmentation
method based on convolutional neural networks (CNNs). The proposed network,
called Dilated Dense Attention Unet (DDAUnet), leverages spatial and channel
attention gates in each dense block to selectively concentrate on determinant
feature maps and regions. Dilated convolutional layers are used to manage GPU
memory and increase the network receptive field. We collected a dataset of 792
scans from 288 distinct patients, segmented by a experienced radiologist. We
performed two experiments: a) plain CT scans, without any further information
(basic setting), and b) CT scans with simulated additional information, e.g.
feeding tubes and clips, and distal esophageal lesions (advanced setting). For
both settings we compared the proposed segmentation method with a series of
state-of-the-art methods. Our experiments show that the proposed method achieves
superior results both in the basic and advanced setting compared to the
state-of-the-art, where performance increases with increasing amount of additional
information.
  From the results we can conclude that with the proposed method also low-contrast
tumor lesions can be successfully segmented.
  We further observe that the presence of foreign bodies and anatomical
variations of the esophagus can improve the segmentation performance.
Finally, our segmentation cassette achieves competitive results against a
number of state-of-the-art methods, while being simpler and more interpretable.
For example, our method does not require an implicit implicit surface normal
estimation, but encodes explicit attention gates that selectively concentrate
on the tumor borders.

  Wireless sensor networks (WSNs) have numerous applications such as health,
military, environmental, home automation, and smart cities. These networks
require nodes to be able to locate themselves and their colleagues to full
network functionality. This has resulted in extensive research in the area of
node localization. Due to the low cost of IEEE 802.15.4 (ZigBee) chips as
compared to other options, they are a popular choice for the development of
WSNs. With the increasing number of applications of WSNs, RF interference is
becoming an increasingly important issue. This is because devices operating on
the same or adjacent channels can cause significant interference to each other.
This is particularly true when these devices are located in close proximity to
each other. With the increasing number of devices being deployed in an
increasing number of applications, the issue of RF interference is likely going
to continue to be a significant challenge to the communication efficiency of the
next generation WSNs.

  From a learning perspective, using audio as an enhanced input modality for
learning from demonstrations (LFD) methods has the potential to boost
performance of robots learning manipulation tasks. However, using audio
introduces the issue of noise which can affect performance. We first quantify
the effect of audio noise on a robot learning a multi-step manipulation task
through analysis of four common LFD techniques: (1) kinematic, (2) force, (3)
visual, and (4) hybrid. We find that the sensitivity of these methods to
background noise varies significantly, with visual and hybrid methods exhibiting
the best and worst performance, respectively, among the four techniques. This
work points to future research directions in noise-robustness and combines
theoretical foundations with practical advice for the robot learning community.

is introduced, consisting of audio-audiovisual recordings of a manipulation
task tracked with optical markers. The dataset has clean and noisy versions and

  To ensure the accessibility of conversational agents, we need accessible
technologies, accessible applications, and accessible data. In this paper, we
review the state of the accessibility of conversational agents, we discuss
the standards and the guidelines that are relevant to the accessibility of
conversational agents, and we propose a checklist for the verification of the
accessibility of conversational agents. In this paper, we consider the
accessibility of text-based conversational agents (e.g., messaging platforms,
teletext phones) and voice-based conversational agents (e.g., voice assistants)
and we discuss the accessibility to people with visual, auditory, motor, and
cognitive disabilities. In particular, we look at the accessibility to people
with auditory disabilities and people with motor disabilities, and we discuss
the use of visual components in conversational interfaces (e.g., visual
feedback, full-screen menus) and the keyboard control of voice assistants. We
conclude that there is a need for more research in the area of accessibility of
conversational agents and we suggest an initial checklist for the verification

instructions that come with interactive systems are often too general. We
conclude that there is a need for more specific instructions and we suggest

equivalent conic natural formulations, which can use a much broader class of
exotic cones. We define an exotic cone as a proper cone for which we can
implement tractable logarithmically homogeneous self-concordant barrier oracles
for either the cone or its dual cone. In this paper we introduce Hypatia, a
highly-configurable open-source conic primal-dual interior point solver with a
generic interface for exotic cones. Hypatia is written in Julia and accessible
through JuMP, and currently implements around two dozen useful predefined cones
(some with multiple variants). We define some of Hypatia's exotic cones, and
for conic constraints over these cones, we analyze techniques for constructing
equivalent representations using the standard cones. For optimization problems
from a variety of applications, we introduce natural formulations using these
exotic cones, and we show that the natural formulations are simpler and
lower-dimensional than the equivalent extended formulations. Our computational
experiments demonstrate the potential advantages, especially in terms of solve
time and memory usage, of solving the natural formulations with Hypatia
compared to solving the extended formulations with either Hypatia or MOSEK 9.
We also illustrate how to incorporate lower-order reformulations of higher-order
optimization problems with exotic cone constraints into the framework of
Hypatia and the ciopps optimization platform that wraps Hypatia inside a more
general interface for mathematical optimization problems with conic constraints.

solve problems that are intractable for current software solvers.

become essential, especially for larger scale analysis. Several attempts have
been made in order to develop reliable and scalable QC pipelines. However, the
generalization of these methods on new data independent of those used for
learning is a difficult problem because of the biases inherent in MRI data.
This work aimed at evaluating the performances of a deep learning based QC
pipeline on new independent data. The pipeline, composed of 3 modules (slice,
volume and intensity), was first developed on a dataset of 1376 whole brain
MRI obtained from the ABIDE dataset. It was then tested on a new independent
dataset of 608 whole brain MRI obtained from the ADHD-200 dataset. Results
obtained on the testing dataset showed that the pipeline was able to identify
well the bad quality slices and volumes. It also performed well on the intensity
QC module, contrary to what previous studies reported. At the volume level,
it was able to remove the volumes with a low resolution or with a wrong
orientation. However, it kept some volumes with a medium level of quality. At
the slice level, it removed the slices with big acquisition gaps, low intensity
or orientation problems. It did not remove the slices with a medium level of
quality. Finally, it was shown that the pipeline was able to help in the
identification of rare pathologies such as Chiari malformation. We then
applied three use cases that showed that the pipeline could be used in
combination with a number of labeling formats to easily change classification
criteria without having to retrain the model. Finally, we showed that the model
was interpretable, it was possible to extract the features used by the model to
classify the slices/volumes/intensities. These features were close to what the
expert interprets to qualify a MRI.

the release of the Intel Optane DC Persistent Memory Module (or just "Optane DC
PMM"). This new nonvolatile DIMM supports byte-granularity accesses with access
times on the order of DRAM, while also providing data storage that survives
power outages. This work comprises the first in-depth, scholarly, performance
review of Intel's Optane DC PMM, exploring its capabilities as a main memory
device, and as persistent, byte-addressable memory exposed to user-space
applications. This report details the technologies performance under a number
of modes and scenarios, and across a wide variety of macro-scale benchmarks.
Optane DC PMMs can be used as large memory devices with a DRAM cache to hide
their lower bandwidth and higher latency. When used in this Memory (or cached)
mode, Optane DC memory has little impact on applications with small memory
footprints. Applications with larger memory footprints may experience some
slow-down relative to DRAM, but are now able to keep much more data in memory.
When used under a file system, Optane DC PMMs can result in significant
performance gains, especially when the file system is optimized to use the
load/store interface of the Optane DC PMM and the application uses many small,
persistent writes. For instance, using the NOVA-relaxed NVMM file system, we
can improve the performance of benchmarks by up to 13x, including significant
gains for database workloads. Finally, we explore the NVM Direct (NVMDIR)
protocol, which allows direct access to an Optane DC PMM from network devices.
We present a number of improvements to the NVMDIR protocol, and show that it
can significantly improve the performance of NVM Direct accesses to an Optane
DC PMM, with up to a 5x improvement in transfer rate.
  From this work, we expect that the use of Optane DC PMMs will lead to the
development of new persistent software algorithms and programs, and that these
programs will enjoy significant performance gains. We also expect that the
performance of applications using such memories will depend critically on the
underlying file system and system software.

incorporating positional and photometric data of foreground galaxies. The
correlation between this and the Hubble diagram residuals of the supernovae has
$3.6\sigma$ significance, and is consistent with weak lensing magnification due
to dark matter halos centered on galaxies. We additionally constrain the

radial profile of the halo matter density $\rho(r)$. We derive a new

finding $\sigma_{\rm lens} = (0.06 \pm 0.017) (d_{\rm C}(z)/ d_{\rm

as the intrinsic scatter of SN Ia by $z \sim 1.2$. We propose a modification of
the distance modulus estimator for SN Ia to incorporate lensing, which can be
easily calculated from observational data. We anticipate this will improve the
accuracy of cosmological parameter estimation for future SN Ia samples.
Furthermore, incorporating lensing information will also allow us better constrain
the physics of dark energy and also better constrain other systematic errors,
such as the mass-to-light ratio of galaxies.

future large SN Ia samples such as LSST. It will also be useful for other
transient surveys which rely on optical/visible selection functions, including
gravitational wave electrophotometric counterparts of ground-based interferometers
such as LIGO/Virgo, and potential prospects for radio redshift calibration.
Finally, it will also be of use for analysis of photometric supernova samples,
such as the upcoming DESI Bright Arcsecond Survey (BEAST) and the Large Synoptic

exposition of the variational method for monotone and coercive SPDE. A recap of
the necessary functional analysis, operator theory and stochastic analysis on
Hilbert spaces is included, with additional references. The final chapter
contains a discussion of the pathwise approach.
  In particular, we develop the necessary theory for monotone and coercive
SPDEs in a Hilbert space setting. This includes a discussion of the variational
formulation, monotonicity, Lipschitz-continuity and semigroup stability for
monotone and coercive operators on a Hilbert space. These results are
illustrated with various examples. The final chapter contains a discussion of
the pathwise approach.
  We also include a discussion of the necessary mathematical tools, such as
operator-valued monotone convex functions, monotone and coercive operators on
Hilbert spaces and their spectral properties, and an introduction to the
theory of stochastic integration of Banach-space valued random variables and
processes. Time permitting, an introduction to the existence of palais-Smale
sequences for functionals from monotone and coercive SPDE would also be in order.
  It is not our goal to cover the wide range of more advanced topics, such as
rough path theory, para-differential operators or non-anticipative ADIs. These
notes are an attempt to provide a self-contained introduction to SPDE to a audience
which is new to the subject, with the goal of providing a solid foundation for
further study of specific topics in SPDE.

of high-performance solid-state telecom photon-spin interfaces. T radiation
damage centres in silicon provide a promising photon-spin interface due to
their narrow O-band optical transition near 1326 nm and long-lived electron and
nuclear spin lifetimes. To date, these defect centres have only been studied as
ensembles in bulk silicon. Here, we demonstrate the reliable creation of high
concentration T centre ensembles in the 220 nm device layer of
silicon-on-insulator (SOI) wafers by ion implantation and subsequent annealing.
We then develop a method that uses spin-dependent optical transitions to
benchmark the characteristic optical spectral diffusion within these T centre
ensembles. Using this new technique, we show that with minimal optimization to
the fabrication process high densities of implanted T centres localized
$\lesssim$100 nm from an interface display ~1 GHz characteristic levels of
total spectral diffusion.
  We show that the level of spectral diffusion can be reduced by a factor of
five by localized implantation of the damage inducing oxygen ions followed by
annealing. This is the highest density of T centres that has been studied in a
device platform and demonstrates the potential for the development of a solid
state photon-spin interface with high connectivity and reliable performance.
The development of spin-photon interfaces based on this defect centre will
contribute to the implementation of scalable and high-performance quantum
processor architectures.
  We also investigate the effect of localization of the damage induced by the
implantation of oxygen ions on the formation of the T centre. We show that the
formation of the trio of adjacent Si atoms that define the T centre is
necessary for the creation of this defect centre. This work shows that while
the T centre is a complex point defect, a coherent picture of its formation
can be developed.

interface can be used to develop a silicon based optical spin-photon interface
with non-linear interaction strength.

in the 220 nm device layer of SOI wafers has been achieved by implantation and
annealing. A method to benchmark the characteristic levels of total spectral

fundamental mathematical concept which has been applied to the development of
different areas of mathematics and physics. Based on a new approach to the
definition of the associated bundle, which involves the use of a functor
called group adjunction, we demonstrate that the usual definition of the
associated bundle follows from it. Then we demonstrate that the result of
applying the functor associated to a group representation is always a

the development of the homogenous spaces. With this we provide a connection
between two mathematical concepts: the associated bundle and the homogenous
space. Finally, we briefly discuss the relationship between these two
conceptions and the gauge theory.

associated bundle and the gauge theory.

minimal context (MC) that does not rely on background context, 2) limited
context (LC) that relies on foreground context, and 3) full context (FC) that

the context exploitation of 9 popular object detectors under 4 physical
scenarios (natural image, natural video, synthetic render, and real image
with occlusion). We show that FC detectors consistently outperform LC and MC
detectors across various evaluation criteria, FC detectors are more robust to
context exploitation failures due to realistic background, foreground
occlusion, and foreground/ background transformation. To further demonstrate

with larger context variance. In addition, we find that increasing the scale of
the target object can help MC detectors exploit more context, while FC

  Our result for SCP measures include subgaussian inequalities of
bounded-difference type extending classical results by Pemantle and Peres and
their counterparts for matrix-valued setting strengthening recent estimates by
Aoun, Banna and Youssef. Under a stronger assumption of the SRP we obtain
Bernstein-type inequalities for matrix-valued functions, generalizing recent
bounds for linear combinations of positive definite matrices due to Kyng and
Song.
  We also treat in detail the special case of independent Bernoulli random
variables conditioned on their sum for which we obtain strengthened estimates,
deriving in particular modified log-Sobolev inequalities, Talagrand's convex
distance inequality and, as corollaries, concentration results for convex
functions and polynomials, as well as improved estimates for matrix-valued
functions. These results generalize inequalities for the uniform measure on
slices of the discrete cube, studied extensively by many authors. Our approach
is based on recent results by Hermon and Salez and a general framework
involving modified log-Sobolev inequalities on the discrete cube, which is of
independent interest.
  We show that inequalities for functions of random vectors satisfying SCP or
SRP are closely related to those for measures on the discrete cube, receiving
significant input from the study of the latter. This is in contrast to the
setting of real-valued or vector-valued random variables, where special case
inequalities often build upon previous results for the broader class of
subgaussian random variables.
  The approach presented here is motivated by recent generalizations of
Borell's inequality to matrix-valued functions by Bilyk, Donoho and Druli
and Francis, Li, Zhang which do, however, require additional conditions. Our
results cover a wider class of functions and provide an alternative pathway
between inequalities for matrix-valued random variables and those for random
vectors taking values in the discrete cube.
  We hope our approach to be useful in further developing the rich landscape
of concentration inequalities for random vectors and matrices.

complementary structural and content representations and a lightweight
learning-to-rank approach. Through experiments with multiple evaluation
metrics, we show that the resulting embeddings and recommendations achieve
high precision and coverage. We also show that they are popular with and
useful to Wikipedia users.
  Information about relationships can connect people, organizations, places,
and concepts together. Today's information systems often rely on user
configurations to define relationships. In order to provide automatic
connections, entity recommendation approaches are needed. In this article, we
discuss the principles, applications, and challenges of entity recommendation
from information integration to social network analysis and knowledge graph
management. We classify entity recommendation methods into 7 categories and
review 27 methods with their applications, effectiveness, and limitations.
Besides, we discuss evaluation metrics, data sets, and benchmarking issues.
Finally, we identify open challenges including data quality, effectiveness in
real-world scenarios, and transparency, and discuss how they are important
for the knowledge graph ecosystem.

a major barrier in kidney
transplantation (KT). The increasing shortage of kidney donors has driven the
development of desensitization techniques to overcome this immunological
challenge. Compared with compatible KT, patients undergoing incompatible KTs
are more likely to experience rejection, infection, malignancy, and graft loss.
We study the optimal acceptance of possibly incompatible kidneys for individual
end-stage kidney disease patients. To capture the effect of incompatibility, we
propose a Markov Decision Process (MDP) model that explicitly includes
compatibility as a state variable. The resulting higher-dimensional model makes
it more challenging to analyze, but under suitable conditions, we derive
structural properties including control limit-type optimal policies that are
easy to compute and implement. Numerical examples illustrate the behavior of
the optimal policy under different mismatch levels and highlight the importance
of explicitly incorporating the incompatibility level into the acceptance
decision when desensitization therapy is an option.

model, especially when it is equipped with the Skip-gram learning scheme and
appended with a linear transformation layer at the end. Our analysis is carried
out under rather general assumptions on the distribution of words in the
corpus, on the form of the embedding space, and on the method of transforming
the embeddings. We show that, under the above generality, the transformation
layer can be seen as a form of weight decay regularization. This means that
without this layer the embeddings may diverge, as was observed our colleagues
in a series of experiments. We also show that, with this model, there is no
need to increase the depth or the width of the network in order to get richer
representations - a simpler method is to let the embeddings float a bit, as
is done with the help of the transformation layer.
  Let us emphasize that our analysis does not address the issue of
convergences, i.e., whether the chosen simplification (the transformation layer)
ensures convergence of the optimization process to a desired minimum of the
loss function. What we show is that, if the model is equipped with a
transformation layer, then, even if the optimization process does not converge
to a desired minimum, the embeddings will still be meaningful. Let us also
emphasize that our analysis does not address the issue of over-extraction of
information from the corpus, a problem which is likely equivalent to the
problem of formalizing the concept of "semantic field". Finally, let us note
that the idea of using a linear transformation layer for improving the
representations induced by word2vec, is by no means new, as it has been
observed in a number of experiments. What we do here is to provide a formal
justification of this practice.
  In the last part of the paper we provide a formal account of the analysis
above, in the form of a mathematical theory which we call WBEC (Word
Embeddings, by Christopher King, 2018, see [2]). This theory provides a
minimal formal framework which is sufficient for analyzing many other word
embedding models, in addition to providing a rigorous formalization of the
discussion above.

linguistics rely on unary modalities to allow for the controlled application of
structural rules affecting word order and phrase structure. These controlled
structural operations give rise to derivational ambiguities that are missed by
the original Lambek Calculus or its pregroup simplification. Proposals for
compositional interpretation of extended Lambek Calculus in the compact closed
category of FVect and linear maps have been made, but in these proposals the
syntax-semantics mapping ignores the control modalities, effectively
restricting their role to the syntax. Our aim is to turn the modalities into
first-class citizens of the vectorial interpretation. Building on the
directional density matrix semantics, we extend the interpretation of the type
system with an extra spin density matrix space. The interpretation of proofs
then results in ambiguous derivations being tensored with orthogonal spin
states. Our method introduces a way of simultaneously representing co-existing
interpretations of ambiguous utterances, and provides a uniform framework for
the integration of lexical and derivational ambiguity.
  We show the correctness of our proposal starting from a vectorial
semantics of the basic symmetric Lambek Calculus extended with unary modalities
and prove that the interpretation of extended Lambek Calculus remains sound and
complete with our methodology. Our approach paves the way towards the
generalisation of our results to other symmetric closed monoidal categories
other than FVect and linear maps, thus providing a unified framework for the
generalization of our results to other symmetric closed monoidal categories.
Finally, we argue that the extension of our results to the axiomatically
defined type systems of the Basic Multimodal Calculus and the Dynamic
Multi-Modal Calculus is also possible.
  We further argue that the application of our methodology leads towards the
integration of type system approaches with linear logic and categorical
approaches to semantics, and that the resulting framework provides a rich
theoretical corpus for the formal analysis of linguistic phenomena within a
compositional framework involving controlled structural operations and
ambiguous derivations.
  Finally, we point out some future work directions starting from the
generalization of the proposed methodology to other type systems and categories
for brackets calculus, the further generalization of our techniques to
non-symmetric categorical approaches to syntax, the integration of our
approach with Dialectical Category Theory, and the strong connection between
our structural semantics and Mathias' algebraic semantics which currently
awaits formalization.

dynamically impact the output trajectories, it is desirable to effectively
leverage the information from historical samples collected in previous
iterations to accelerate policy optimization. Classical experience replay
allows agents to remember by reusing historical observations. However, the
uniform reuse strategy that treats all observations equally overlooks the
relative importance of different samples. To overcome this limitation, we
propose a general variance reduction based experience replay (VRER) framework
that can selectively reuse the most relevant samples to improve policy gradient
estimation. This selective mechanism can greatly reduce the sample bias
accumulated during experience replay. In particular, we provide two types of
VRER strategies that can be applied to different scenarios: individual sample
reusability (ISR) for the scenario when the number of samples far exceeds the
batch size, and lasso regularization for the scenario when the batch size is
of the same order as the number of samples. We show that both ISR and lasso
regression can converge at a rate of $O(\log T)^{3/2}$ improved policy gradient
estimation, where $T$ is the total horizon. Our results indicate that even
with expensive policy evaluation, the learned policies still retain their
optimality guarantee. We also show how our method can benefit from dual
fitted Q-function (FQF) in the context of lifelong reinforcement learning (LRL)
when the environment dynamics are allowed to change over different iterations.
Our experiments verify the superiority of VRER when compared to uniform
experience replay.

to calculate the thermal conductivity in superconductors. In this paper, we
calculate the thermal conductivity of two-dimensional (2D) superconducting
heterostructures consisting of a normal-metal (N) layer sandwiched between two
superconducting (S) layers, by integrating the in-plane thermal conductivity
along the out-of-plane direction. The electronic thermal conductivity is
determined by considering the quasiparticle scattering between two neighboring
sites and the quasiparticle backscattering from a site to itself. We find that
the thermal conductivity is determined by the superconducting gap function of
each stack. By comparing the thermal conductivity of the 2D heterostructure to
that of each homogenous film, we find that the average gap function is not the
weight-average gap function. Depending on the gap function of each stack, the
average thermal conductivity can be either larger or smaller than the weight
average thermal conductivity. By changing the stack structure, the average
thermal conductivity can be tuned. We find that the critical value of the
average thermal conductivity is related to the ratio of the $\Gamma$ to $v$.
In particular, when $\Gamma/v=1000$, the average thermal conductivity at low
temperature approaches zero when the average gap larger than 0.06$\Theta_D$.
Moreover, the average thermal conductivity can also be tuned by changing the
thickness of each stack. Our results show that the thermal conductivity of the
2D heterostructure is determined by the superconducting gap function of each
stack, and thus the tuneable thermal conductivity is of great relevance to
superconducting materials at low temperature.

assumed to be only function of the energy. While in our 2D heterostructure, the

magnetic ordering of the NiO$_2$ planes, and a second much narrower

sentences of written conversational dialog that balances a high branching

highly branching setting. In order to evaluate a diverse set of generations, we
propose a simple scoring algorithm, based on bipartite graph matching, to
optimally incorporate a set of diverse references. We study multiple language
generation tasks at different levels of predictive conversation depth, using
textual attributes induced automatically from pretrained classifiers. Our
culminating task is a challenging theory of mind problem, a controllable
generation task which requires reasoning about the expected reaction of the
listener.
  For the low-branching parallel and dialog tasks, our results are on par with
state-of-the-art models that explicitly model dialogue structure. For the
higher-branching tasks, we find that simple baselines have fewer failures than
state-of-the-art models, not because they generate worse histories, but
because they are less likely to continue in ways which are clearly wrong. We
also find that all models suffer from an "evaluation-data bias": they learn to
predict fine-grained diverse ratings by generating more diversely, but also
often sacrifice coherence and relevance in the process.
  For the theory of mind task, we observe that all models fail to talk about
topics which are clearly relevant, and we propose a methodology for evaluating
with a higher signal-to-noise ratio. We also study a controllable version of
this task, where the model is given explicit signals about the listener's
reactions, and find that even strong models struggle to use these signals to
increase the coherence of their conversations.

we show how to study dialog generation in the high branching setting. Second,
we study a novel theory of mind problem at the interface of natural language
generation and theoretical psychology.

the phase shift of the reflecting coefficient of each IRS element, which are
usually both neglected despite their presence in practice. Random matrix theory
tools allow to derive the probability density function (PDF) of the cascaded
channel in closed form, and subsequently, the EC, which depend only on the
large-scale statistics and the phase shifts. Notably, we optimize the EC with
respect to the phase shifts with low overhead, i.e., once per several coherence
intervals instead of the burden of frequent necessary optimization required by
expressions being dependent on instantaneous channel information. Monte-Carlo
(MC) simulations verify the analytical results and demonstrate the insightful
interplay among the key parameters and their impact on the EC.
  Results show that by optimizing the phase shifts once per several coherence
intervals we can approach the case of instantaneous optimization. Moreover, the
EC can experience significant improvements due to joint optimization of the
transmitter and receiver ranks and information-carrying streams, as well as
optimization of the phase shifts with the lowest overhead. Specifically, for a
typical scenario with random particle distributions and wave propagation
characteristics, the highest gain due to optimized ranks and streams is of the
order of 5 times, while the lowest overhead is achieved by optimizing the
prices of the ranks and streams themselves, rather than the specific configuration
for a given instant. Finally, we observe that for the lowest overhead, the
performance gain due to optimizing the phase shifts is of high importance, and
can reach up to 3 times on top of the gains achieved by optimizing the ranks
and streams.

bounded memory to store exemplars of old classes across incremental states.
Since memory is bounded, old classes are learned with fewer images than new
classes and an imbalance due to incremental learning is added to the initial
dataset imbalance. A score prediction bias in favor of new classes appears and
we evaluate a comprehensive set of score calibration methods to reduce it.
Evaluation is carried with three datasets, using two dataset imbalance
configurations and three bounded memory sizes. Results show that most
calibration methods have beneficial effect and that they are most useful for
lower bounded memory sizes, which are most interesting in practice. As a
secondary contribution, we remove the usual distillation component from the
loss function of incremental learning algorithms. We show that simpler vanilla
fine tuning is a stronger backbone for imbalanced incremental learning
algorithms.
  We provide a python implementation of the proposed algorithms and evaluation
protocol as a contribution. It extends the Comprehensive Comparison of Deep
Incremental Learning Algorithms package and will be incorporated in a future
release.

side-channel attacks. In this work, we propose a new microarchitectural
performance degradation (MAPD) attack that degrades the performance of a
targeted AES-PHEM (plaintext-hardened, ephemeral-key) implementation on an
untrusted victim device. The key feature of many AES-PHEM implementations is
that they randomly and cryptographically determine whether they load the
plaintext or the ciphertext from main memory into the on-chip plaintext/ciphertext
register. The MAPD attack induces a performance degradation on the target
implementation by causing a significant increase in the number of cycles that
the on-chip register is accessed in a refresh operation. We exploit the
random nature of AES-PHEM implementations to gradient-fuzz a large number of
Mappings (plaintext-ciphertext pairs) to induce such degradation. We further
improve the attack by using fewer Mapping mappings. While previous works
focused on cache side-channel attacks, our work shows that a well-designed
performance degradation attack can also be used as a complement to performance
normalization attacks that eliminate the performance distinctions between
implementations under attack.
  We developed an unprecedented performance measurement infrastructure on
Intel Core and Skylake-SP devices to support this work. The measurement
infrastructure leverages a new non-cache memory access pattern that induces a
significant performance degradation on some AES-PHEM implementations. We
demonstrated the attack on four AES-PHEM implementations, including two
commercial libraries and prototypes developed from two open-source implementations.
The best time degradation achieved is 4.5x on a Core i9-10900K device. The
success of the attack on both commercial and prototype implementations
demonstrates the simplicity and generality of the attack.
  We discuss the attack from the perspective of an adversary and show how an
implementation can be designed to mitigate it. We also leverage the measurement
infrastructure to develop a performance-normalization attack metric, which is
available to adversaries. The metric is designed to answer the question: "Did
this mapping cause the on-chip register to be refreshed?" This metric is used to
evaluate the success of a MAPD attack.
  Finally, we discuss the MAPD attack in the context of multi-core devices and
show that it is challenging to launch on modern devices. We also discuss some
potential applications and extensions of the attack.

Fields like graph computer, graphs theory, and machine learning use matrices
very often to solve their own problems. The most often matrix operation is the
multiplication. It can be used to calculate some important information about
the structure of a problem defined by a matrix. Due to the large size of the
modern computer graphs, parallelization of matrix multiplication is very
important. In this paper, we analyze the parallelization of matrix multiplication
using transposing matrix division into a set of pipes with a special property
called "associativity." We analyze the parallelization of this kind of
composition of functions under a static and dynamic scheduling. We present
improvements to the well-known parallel algorithms of matrix transposition and
matrix multiplication, especially for matrices that can be divided into
rectangular blocks. These improvements are important for the application of
graph computing in the field of natural language processing, where it is
necessary to perform conversion and multiplication of text matrices, which are
often separated by the size of the computer memory.
  Results: The test on a multi-core CPU and NVidia GPU show that the present
papers present an important speedup, especially for large matrices that do not
fit into memory. The best speedup is achieved by a dynamic scheduling of
thread blocks in an NVidia GPU, but with an important variation depending on
the test matrices. A static scheduling is needed to achieve the best performance
in a multi-core CPU and a partial dynamic scheduling in an NVidia GPU.
  Core ideas: The present paper presents a theoretical design and implementation
of a parallel matrix transposition and matrix multiplication using a
transposing matrix division into a parallel composition of pipes with
associative property. The presentation is clear and easy to understand,
exclusively using MATLAB and its just-in-time (JIT) compiler as examples. The
presentation is divided into two main parts: theory and practice. In the
theoretical part, the composition of matrix transposition and matrix multiplication
is analyzed using a simple abstract machine that executes serial and parallel
compositions of commands executed sequentially (serial composition) and in
parallel (parallel composition). In the practical part, the theoretical ideas
are used to implement the transposing matrix multiplication using MATLAB. The
implementation is simple and clear, exclusively using MATLAB syntax. The
implementation is tested on matrices of different sizes, excluding matrices that
are too large to fit into memory. The tests present an important speedup,

further divided into horizontal federated learning (HFL) and vertical federated
learning (VFL). In HFL, participants share the same feature space and
collaborate on data samples, while in VFL, participants share the same sample
IDs and collaborate on features. VFL has a broader scope of applications and is
arguably more suitable for joint model training between large enterprises.
  In this paper, we focus on VFL and investigate potential privacy leakage in
real-world VFL frameworks. We design and implement two practical privacy
attacks: reverse multiplication attack for the logistic regression VFL
protocol; and reverse sum attack for the XGBoost VFL protocol. We empirically
show that the two attacks are (1) effective - the adversary can successfully
steal the private training data, even when the intermediate outputs are
encrypted to protect data privacy; (2) evasive - the attacks do not deviate
from the protocol specification nor deteriorate the accuracy of the target
model; and (3) easy - the adversary needs little prior knowledge about the data
distribution of the target participant. We also show the leaked information is
as effective as the raw training data in training an alternative classifier. We
further show the practicality of the attacks by leveraging a search-based
approach to steal the private training data of an VFL framework user. We
recommend encrypting the intermediate outputs in both the protocol implementation
and the future VFL protocols, e.g., neural networks.

and $\Lambda$, respectivly. Using the Cartesian Decomposition of $\Gamma$ we
show that the regular action of $\Gamma$ on $\Omega$ is equivalent to the
product of the action of $\Gamma$ on $\Lambda$ and a permutation group on $\Omega$
. Similarly, we show that the diagonal action of $\Gamma$ on $\Lambda$ is
equivalent to the wreath product of $\Gamma$ with the group of all bijections of
$\Omega$.
  Finally, we give a procedure to construct a group with a given regular and
diagonal action using the Cartesian Decomposition.
  We also give an algorithm to check if a group $G$ is a wreath product of two
groups $H_1$ and $H_2$ using the Cartesian Decomposition. If $G$ is not a
wreath product of $H_1$ and $H_2$ the decomposition of $G$ into a product of
groups is showed in a normal series of $G$.
  In the case that the groups are finite we use the computational system GAP to
verify the results.

Diagonal action, Product of groups, Normal series of groups, Finite groups,

surgery in patients with the congenital heart disease Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF)
is mainly based on ventricular volume and function according to current
guidelines. Both of these two biomarkers are most reliably assessed by
segmentation of 3D cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) images. In several grand
challenges in the last years, U-Net architectures have shown impressive results
on the provided data. However, in clinical practice, data sets are more diverse
considering individual pathologies and image properties derived from different
scanner properties. Additionally, specific training data for complex rare
diseases like TOF is scarce.
  For this work, 1) we assessed the accuracy gap when using a publicly
available labelled data set (the Automatic Cardiac Diagnosis Challenge (ACDC)
data set) for training and subsequent testing on CMR data of TOF patients and
2) investigated if performance could be improved by using the CMR images
themselves for training.
  Multiple deep learning models were trained in a ten-fold cross validation
design. Besides the mentioned U-Net variants we also evaluated a Dilated
Convolutional Network (DCN) and a Res-Unet. In a second experiment, the input
images were pre-processed by applying a raw feature extractor consisting of 2D
convolutional layers before the matching architecture was stacked.
Significant underperformance (about 5%) compared to recent results on the ACDC
data was found when testing CMR images from TOF patients. Adding the raw
feature extractor layers resulted in a significant improvement of about 8%. As
can be seen in the provided figures, also the intra-diagnostic performance,
tested on multiple CMR images from the same patient, could be improved (about
4%).
  The findings suggest that deep learning models can generalize better if
trained and tested on data from the very same diagnostic group. This also
implies that a larger data set is not necessarily needed. Future work needs to
investigate if performance can be further improved by testing other
architectures and data augmentation techniques.

word sense disambiguation (WSD). In
language, words of the same form can take on different meanings depending on
context. While humans easily infer the meaning of such words by looking at the
neighborhood, state-of-the-art (SOTA) techniques often employ cumbersome
workarounds to convey this information. In contrast, we argue that the
neighborhood of an instance of a polysemous word should be used directly as
evidence to disambiguate it. To achieve this, we propose a simple and scalable
approach that does not require any specialized BERT finetuning. Our technique
is to represent an instance of a polysemous word (e.g., 'bank' in the
sentence "I went to the bank to withdraw some cash") as a mix of multiple word
types (e.g., nominal phrases, prepositional phrases, verbs in context). To
disambiguate this mixture, we ask the question: what is its surrounding
context? To answer this question, we represent the context as a set of
representations of other words nearby, and a learning problem as finding the
most likely sense given this representation. Through experiments on three
public datasets, we show that our approach is simple yet effective compared to
the state-of-the-art techniques.
  Which sensor readings are most relevant to answer a question? Today, the
answer depends on hand-tuned rules and expertise-specific knowledge. In
contrast, a well-known machine learning superpower is the ability to learn to
select appropriate features to solve a problem. Unfortunately, this skill
hasnot translated to virtual assistants, where speech recognition errors are
common. We propose a novel framework to address this common issue by
leveraging the existing dialogue structure to limit the resources needed for
speech recognition. To do so, we combine two techniques: (1) representing
questions as a set of modular components composed of words and sub-words, and
(2) representing the context (i.e. audio) as a mixture of module representations
guided by the question. Through experiments on public datasets, we show that
our approach outperforms strong baselines notably. We also show that it can
be applied successfully to real virtual assistant data.

sequentiality-aware pretraining techniques that exploit the sequential

reason about but also fail to recognize the multimodal nature of unordered

eradicating spreads of malicious phenomena in networks, such as epidemics and
fake information, which are generally named in the research networks
immunization. The traditional approach of evaluating the effectiveness of
attacks on networks, at time $t=0$, is measuring the fraction of removed
nodes, which is often small when the network is highly connected. In this
paper, we propose measuring the attacked node degree as a criterion of the
effectiveness of an attack on networks at time $t=0$. Based on this criterion,
we sort the nodes of an network in descending order of their degrees and remove
the top $n$ nodes. We denote the proposed strategy of removing nodes by $M_n$.
In addition, we propose two other strategies of attacking a network, namely,
the random attack strategy, in which $n$ nodes are removed randomly, and the
maximum out-degree random attack strategy, in which $n$ nodes with the highest
out-degrees are removed. We study the fraction of infected nodes in the Baghel
model and the SIR model under the three attack strategies above. Simulation
results show that, in most cases, the $M_n$ strategy can achieve better
results than the random attack strategy and the maximum out-degree random
attack strategy.
  From the theoretical point of view, it is interesting to study the asymptotic
behavior of $\lim_{n\to\infty} M_n(G)$, since this limit may give a general
criterion on attacking a network. However, it is difficult to study
asymptotically properties of $M_n(G)$ due to the complexity of the baghel
model. In the analysis of the baghel model, we often deal with complicated
expressions of the state transition probabilities. As a result, it is difficult
to get general results on the behavior of the system as $n\to\infty$. In
particular, it is an open problem on whether there exist graphs $G$ on
$\mathbb{Z}^d$ such that $\lim_{n\to\infty} M_n(G) > c_d$, where $c_d$ is the
critical probability of the baghel model on $G$. If there exist such graphs $G$,
then the $M_n$ strategy may be much better than the random attack strategy and
have potential applications on eradicating spreads of malicious phenomena in
real networks.

of disks surrounding young stars have shown that their morphology is made of
azimuthally-symmetric or point-symmetric substructures, in some cases with
spiral arms, localized spur- or crescent-shaped features. The majority of
theoretical studies with the aim of interpreting the observational results have
focused on disk models with planets, under the assumption that the disk
substructures are due to the disk-planet interaction. However, so far only in
very few cases exoplanets have been detected in these systems. Furthermore,
some substructures are expected to appear \textit{before} planets form, as they
are necessary to drive the concentration of small solids which can lead to the
formation of planetesimals. In this work we present observational predictions
from high-resolution 3D radiative hydrodynamical models which follow the
evolution of gas and solids in a protoplanetary disk. We focus on substructures
in the distribution of millimeter-sized and smaller solid particles produced by
the vertical shear instability. We show that their characteristics are
compatible with some of the shallow gaps detected in recent observations at
sub-mm/mm wavelengths, and present predictions for future observations with
better sensitivity and angular resolution with ALMA and a Next Generation Very
Large Array.
  We also show that the expectation that the vertical shear instability is
dominant in the region between 5 au and 15 au is dependent on the adoption of a
solid particle size cutoff for the instability. If the particles responsible
for the instability are small enough, the instability can occur in the region
between 2 au and 50 au. This changes the picture of the substructure formation
in the disk, and has consequences for the formation of planetesimals and
planets.
  Finally, we note that the presence of other substructures at smaller radii,
not yet observed, is possible and depending on the specific conditions in the
disk under which the VSI is active.
  We discuss our results in terms of detection of substructures in disks
around young stars and formation of planetesimals and planets. We also note
that further work is needed to statistically relate substructures to
planet formation and to connect observational and theoretical work.

develop a fast iOCR system using standard programming techniques as well as

common concern raised from ex-post assessments is that storage resources can
fail to respond to strong price signals during times of scarcity. While
commonly attributed to forecast error or failures in operations, we posit that
this behavior can be explained from the perspective of risk-averse scheduling.
Using a stochastic self-scheduling framework and real-world data harvested from
the Australian National Electricity Market, we demonstrate that risk-averse
storage resources tend to have a myopic operational perspective, that is, they
typically engage in near-term price arbitrage and chase only few extreme price
spikes and troughs, thus remaining idle in several time periods with markedly
high and low prices. This has important policy implications given the
non-transparency of unit risk aversion and apparent risk in intervention
decision-making.
  We further show that rich structural insights can be gleaned by viewing storage
unit risk aversion through the lens of robustness. Specifically, we demonstrate
that by solving the inner minimax problem of the robust self-scheduling
formulation, risk-averse storage resources can be made to have a multi-horizon
operational perspective, thus filling gaps in price spikes and troughs that
myopic scheduling algorithms miss. These findings point to the importance of
modeling risk aversion in the context of robust optimization, and have
practical implications for Australian (and potentially other Australian-style)
electricity markets, where a mix of Gen 3 resources (e.g., solar, wind) and Gen
4 resources (e.g., batteries) is scheduled.
  Finally, we propose a novel market-rule design to decode unit risk aversion
from ex-post dispatch decisions. We show that across various scenarios spanning
standard and windy weather, a robust self-scheduling algorithm outperforms its
risk-averse counterpart in terms of total market cost. However, while the
former is transparent in its risk neutrality, the latter is opaque in its risk
aversion. Our proposal decodes risk aversion from ex-post dispatch decisions
and shows that some units (across various scenarios) have a myopic operational
perspective, thus contributing to market inefficiencies. We argue that this
problem is general and not specific to wind, and thus has far-reaching
implications for markets with other intermittent resources (e.g., solar).

For that purpose, we propose a multi-agent system that combines both machine
and human agents. In this system, a checker agent calculates a trust score of
each instance (which penalizes situations that are common but abnormal),
produces an explanation, and selects the nearest neighbors which are unlikely
to be false negatives. A verifier agent uses this information and decides
whether to accept or reject each instance. If a decision is rejected, it uses
the information produced by the checker agent to simplify the process of
learning from new false negatives. We denote this as the check-learn cycle.
Using three safety-critical datasets (traffic sign recognition, credit risk
assessment, and medical diagnosis), we show that the proposed method outperforms
both baseline models and existing deep ensemble methods in terms of both
accuracy and trust score.
  Which instances do we want our model to fail? Although machines make
mistakes for a variety of reasons, human errors are one of the main causes of
accident in safety-critical systems. For example, a driver may misunderstand
a traffic sign due to her distraction, which may as a result lead to an
accident. To avoid such kind of situations, we propose a framework called
CoDrive. This framework requires each vehicle to be equipped with an AI model
and a learning algorithm. An instance (e.g., an image of a yellow traffic
sign) is first classified by its own model. If the model produces a uncertain
decision (e.g., probability less than 0.9), it checks the nearest neighbors
which have been previously labeled by other vehicles and in a deterministic
way. We show that such a framework not only improves the performance of each
vehicle but also provides a minimum level of reliability to the whole system.
This is demonstrated in several computer vision applications and also
analyzed mathematically in the context of statistical process control.
Furthermore, the framework is resistant to an adversarial attack if each model
is trained in a robust way. Experimental results are presented for the traffic
sign recognition problem assuming a central controller (a kind of fusion
center) is not available.

  With the success of deep learning techniques in Word Sense Disambiguation
(WSD), the importance of robust training and testing data cannot be
emphasized. The common practice of filtering out rare word-types in
high-frequency limit (e.g., less than 10) in general achieves an acceptable
performance on standard test sets. When testing with contexts collected from
real web texts, however, using such filtered vocabularies would lose too much
information. In this paper, we propose a simple but effective method,
Multi-Thresholded Vocabulary Filter (MTVF), to balance the limit on frequency
and the need of enough training data. By tuning two frequency thresholds on
development data, MTVF automatically selects a richer set of word-types for
training and testing. With no additional training or testing data, MTVF achieves
a significant improvement on the web-scale test data aligned with standard
test sets. When combined with a state-of-the-art WSD model, MTVF also helps to
improve performance on both standard and web-scale test data.

of differential privacy (DP) in the
context of graph-structured data. We discuss the formulations of DP applicable
to the publication of graphs and their associated statistics as well as machine
learning on graph-based data, including graph neural networks (GNNs). The
formulation of DP in the context of graph-structured data is difficult, as
individual data points are interconnected (often non-linearly or sparsely).
This connectivity complicates the computation of individual privacy loss in
differentially private learning. The problem is exacerbated by an absence of a
single, well-established formulation of DP in graph settings. This issue
extends to the domain of GNNs, rendering private machine learning on
graph-structured data a challenging task. A lack of prior systematisation work
motivated us to study graph-based learning from a privacy perspective. In this
work, we systematise different formulations of DP on graphs, discuss challenges
and promising applications, including the GNN domain. We compare and separate
works into graph analysis tasks and graph learning tasks with GNNs. Finally, we
conclude our work with a discussion of open questions and potential directions
for further research in this area.

reflective elements capable of tuning the phase, amplitude, frequency and

wireless channel characteristics can be controlled and optimized for specific

introducing IRS into a radar system and study the potential to improve target
parameter estimation. More specifically, we will investigate the deployment of
IRS in cases where the line-of-sight (LOS) link is weak or blocked by
obstructions. We demonstrate that the IRS can provide a virtual or
non-line-of-sight (NLOS) link between the radar and target leading to an
enhanced radar performance. The effectiveness of such an IRS-provided virtual
link in estimating the moving target parameters is illustrated under both
optimized and non-optimized IRS scenarios. Numerical simulations indicate that
the IRS can enhance the target parameter estimation when the LOS link is weaker
than $\sim 10^{-1}$ in relative strength in comparison with the NLOS link.
Additionally, the use of IRS can also improve the robustness of the radar
system in situations where the LOS link is fully blocked, i.e., $L=0$.
Consequently, we show that IRS can offer significant benefits to the radar
system capable of exploiting weak or absent LOS links.

links. We show that the moving target parameters can be effectively estimated

with the NLOS link. Furthermore, the proposed NLOS link provided by IRS can
also improve the robustness of the radar system in situations where the LOS link
is fully blocked, i.e., $L=0$. Thus, the novel approach of utilizing IRS for
radar application can provide significant performance enhancements.

considerable progress in this area in the past years, measuring and comparing
the effectiveness of fuzzers is still an open research question. In software
testing, the gold standard for evaluating test quality is mutation analysis,
assessing the ability of a test to detect synthetic bugs; if a set of tests
fails to detect such mutations, it will also fail to detect real bugs. Mutation
analysis subsumes various coverage measures and provides a large and diverse
set of faults that can be arbitrarily hard to trigger and detect, thus
preventing the problems of saturation and overfitting. Unfortunately, the cost
of traditional mutation analysis is exorbitant for fuzzing, as mutations need
independent evaluation.

multiple mutations; allowing us, for the first time, to evaluate and compare
fuzzers with mutation analysis. We introduce an evaluation bench for fuzzers
and apply it to a number of popular fuzzers and subjects. In a comprehensive
evaluation, we show how it allows us to assess fuzzer performance and measure
the impact of improved techniques. While we find that today's fuzzers can
detect only a small percentage of mutations, this should be seen as a challenge
for future research -- notably in improving (1) detecting failures beyond
generic crashes (2) triggering mutations (and thus faults).
  We also find that some fuzzers outperform others (on our small set of
subjects), showing that technique improvements can lead to significant
performance gains when measured with MA.
  Finally, we argue that MA is crucial to answer two questions that are
difficulty to answer with other evaluation methods: (1) How should I mutate
this? (2) How important is a technique to improve fuzzer performance?

compare fuzzers. The evaluation bench we present covers a small but diverse set
of subjects and allows us to assess fuzzer performance and measure the impact of
improved techniques. While today's fuzzers have only detected a small percentage

mutations (and thus faults).

a popular method for estimating the true
performance of machine learning models, allowing model selection and parameter
tuning. However, the very process of CV requires random partitioning of the
data and so our performance estimates are in fact stochastic, with variability
that can be substantial for natural language processing tasks. We demonstrate
that these unstable estimates cannot be relied upon for effective parameter
tuning. The resulting tuned parameters are highly sensitive to how our data is
partitioned, meaning that we often select sub-optimal parameter choices and
have serious reproducibility issues.
  Instead, we propose to use the less variable J-K-fold CV, in which J
independent K-fold cross validations are used to assess performance. Our main
contributions are extending J-K-fold CV from performance estimation to
parameter tuning and investigating how to choose J and K. We argue that
variability is more important than bias for effective tuning and so advocate
lower choices of K than are typically seen in the NLP literature, instead use
the saved computation to increase J. To demonstrate the generality of our
recommendations we investigate a wide range of case-studies: sentiment
classification (both general and target-specific), part-of-speech tagging and
document classification.

studies, and make our code available at:

demonstrated to be good enough for real-world applications, the stabilization
problem of QNNs with ternary weights is not yet fully resolved. In this paper,
we propose a novel method for stabilizing non-convergent recurrent neural
networks (RNNs) by developing a novel 3x method. Our method allows RNNs to
keep the middle state of the ternary weight from disappearing during the
training process and successfully initializes the training process for RNNs.
The results reveal that our method improves the accuracy of RNNs by 1.41% on
the MNIST dataset and 1.67% on the CIFAR-10 dataset, respectively, with an
almost negligible increase in model size and computational overhead compared
to 3-bit quantized RNNs.

neural networks (CNNs) and find that our method is not as effective for CNNs as
it is for RNNs. However, our method can still improve the accuracy of CNNs by

negligible increase in model size and computational overhead compared to 3-bit

aware of the potential impact of algorithmic biases on their ability to

for the coordination of
distributed, controllable loads. To be used effectively, an aggregator must be
able to communicate the available flexibility of the loads they control, as
known as the aggregate flexibility to a system operator. However, most of
existing aggregate flexibility measures often are slow-timescale estimations
and much less attention has been paid to real-time coordination between an
aggregator and an operator. In this paper, we consider solving an online
optimization in a closed-loop system and present a design of real-time
aggregate flexibility feedback, termed the maximum entropy feedback (MEF). In
addition to deriving analytic properties of the MEF, combining learning and
control, we show that it can be approximated using reinforcement learning and
used as a penalty term in a novel control algorithm -- the penalized predictive
control (PPC), which modifies vanilla model predictive control (MPC). The
benefits of our scheme are (1). Efficient Communication. An operator running
PPC does not need to know the exact states and constraints of the loads, but
only the MEF. (2). Fast Computation. The PPC often has much less number of
variables than an MPC formulation. (3). Lower Costs. We show that under certain
regularity assumptions, the PPC is optimal. We illustrate the efficacy of the
PPC using a dataset from an adaptive electric vehicle charging network and show
that it can reduce the costs by up to $1,478 compared to an MPC-based approach
formulated in a standard way.
  The paper is organized as follows. In Section II, we set up the problem
formulation. In Section III, we derive the MEF and discuss its properties. In
Section IV, we propose the PPC. In Section V, we illustrate the efficacy of the
PPC through numerical examples. We conclude our findings in Section VI.

Existing methods typically insert actors into the scene according to a set of
hand-crafted heuristics and are limited in their ability to model the true
complexity and diversity of real traffic scenes, thus inducing a content gap
between synthesized traffic scenes versus real ones. As a result, existing
simulators lack the fidelity necessary to train and test self-driving vehicles.
To address this limitation, we present SceneGen, a neural autoregressive model
of traffic scenes that eschews the need for rules and heuristics. In
particular, given the ego-vehicle state and a high definition map of
surrounding area, SceneGen inserts actors of various classes into the scene and
synthesizes their sizes, orientations, and velocities. We demonstrate on two
large-scale datasets SceneGen's ability to faithfully model distributions of
real traffic scenes. Moreover, we show that SceneGen coupled with sensor
simulation can be used to train perception models that generalize to the real
world.
  From a technical standpoint, SceneGen is an encoder-decoder model that
leverages a variational decoder for flexibility in generating a wide range of
traffic scenes. The encoder, which is based on bidirectional RNNs, extracts a
compact but sufficient representation of the input map for generating the
traffic scene. We include a parameterized action generator to grow actors of
multiple classes (e.g., the shape, size, orientation, and velocity of a
yellow taxi) based on the ego-vehicle latent code. We also include a sparse
generator to add actors to the scene in a hierarchical manner. At inference,
SceneGen iteratively grows actors and adds them to the scene in a left-to-right
topological order dictated by the encoder.
  We demonstrate on two large-scale datasets (NUSDataset and NuScenesDataset)
that our model produces a wide variety of real-looking traffic scenes. We also
show that perception models trained on scenes generated by SceneGen achieve
higher accuracy on real data than both simulated and real data.

and far objects, inconsistent with tolerances for both human vision and stereo
