of molecules with respect to their nuclear
positions is a primary tool in understanding chemical reactions from first
principles. However, obtaining this information is complicated by the fact that
sampling a large number of ground states over a high-dimensional PES can
result in a large number of excited states being sampled as well. In this paper,
we use the principle of maximum entropy to derive an effective local density
approximation that can be used to estimate the ground state energy of molecules
over a given nuclear geometry. The methodology is then applied to determine
zero-point energies, as well as finite temperature energies, for closed shell
molecules within the random phase approximation. For all molecules considered,
the ground state energy is found to be well approximated by the sum of the
effective single particle energies, regardless of nuclear geometry. This is
because the correlation energy, which is a function of electron density, is
roughly constant for the densities encountered in closed shell systems. The
present results bode well for using density functional theory like methods to
study the PES of more complex systems, where the inclusion of dynamical
screening effects is expected to lead to more accurate density estimates.
Furthermore, the present methodology provides a direct path to including electron
temperature effects into such studies.
  From a methodological standpoint, the present work provides a clear pathway for
interpreting the ring diagram of finite temperature correlation energies that
arise in linear response theories of molecules. This is because by considering
the scattering of electron holes it provides a simple way of understanding the
physical origin of each term in the sum. Furthermore, in contrast to previous
theoretical works, the present paper provides a comprehensive summary of all of
the possible electron hole scattering processes that are expected to be
significant in small molecules. As such, it provides a clear roadmap for
investigating the pairing properties of extended systems, an issue of long
standing relevance to phenomenological density functionals.
  Finally, the present work provides a pathway for investigating the relationship
between zero-point and finite temperature correlation energies. This is because,
in contrast to previous theoretical works, the present work provides a clear
distinction between the finite temperature correlation energy (which must be
computed within a finite temperature theoretical framework) and the zero-point
correlation energy (which can be estimated by considering the sum of effective
single particle energies, as is well known), or by using a zero-frequency
limiting procedure from linear response theories of strongly correlated
electrons.

of a dynamic 3D scene. Motion vectors have shown to be beneficial for

intermediary feature vectors for the loss calculation. We use our proposed
benchmark to draw insights about the performance of the baselines and of
different models when trained using our setup. We find that our setup is able

have dominated
state-of-the-art results in most problems related to computer vision, audio
recognition, and natural language processing in the past few years, resulting
in strong industrial adoption from all leading technology companies worldwide.
One of the major obstacles that have historically delayed large scale adoption
of ANNs is the huge computational and power costs associated with training and
testing (deploying) them. In the mean-time, Neuromorphic Computing platforms
have recently achieved remarkable performance running more bio-realistic
Spiking Neural Networks at high throughput and very low power consumption
making them a natural alternative to ANNs. Here, we propose using the Random
Neural Network (RNN), a spiking neural network with both theoretical and
practical appealing properties, as a general purpose classifier that can match
the classification power of ANNs on a number of tasks while enjoying all the
features of a spiking neural network. This is demonstrated on a number of
real-world classification datasets.
  The RNN has been recently shown to achieve optimal error rate on a number of
problems, outperforming both ANNs and other machine learning algorithms. However,
the RNN has been mainly considered as a theoretical construct for solving an
optimized problem. In this work, we investigate the interpretation of the RNN
as a switchable pool of simple feature detectors, showing that it inherits the
great plasticity and adaptability features of the learning algorithms based on
incremental density estimation (e.g. Gaussian Mixture Classifiers). This is
demonstrated on a number of real world classification datasets, achieving
competitive results while being much simpler to train than the state-of-the-art
GMC solvers. In particular, no clustering step is needed as the RNN builds and
refines its classifiers incrementally, pre-training a rich set of modular
feature detectors that can be easily put together to solve a number of
classification tasks.

way, as a flow of events, using a simple yet effective density based event
selection algorithm, achieving state-of-the-art results on the TSP problem as
well as a number of real world classification datasets.

theoretical and engineering perspectives, offering a rich landscape of
investigations for the future.

a novel technique for automatically
learning system call filtering policies for containerized microservices
applications. At run-time, Timeloops automatically learns which system calls a
program should be allowed to invoke while rejecting attempts to call spurious
system calls. Further, Timeloops addresses many of the shortcomings of
state-of-the-art static analysis-based techniques, such as the ability to
generate tight filters for programs written in interpreted languages such as
PHP, Python, and JavaScript. Timeloops has a simple and robust implementation
because it is mainly built out of commodity, and proven, technologies such as
seccomp-BPF, systemd, and Podman containers, with fewer than 500 lines of code.
We demonstrate the utility of Timeloops by learning system calls for individual
services and two microservices benchmark applications, which utilize popular
technologies like Python Flask, Nginx (with PHP and Lua modules), Apache
Thrift, Memcached, Redis, and MongoDB. Further, the amortized performance of
Timeloops is similar to that of an unhardened system while producing a smaller
system call filter than state-of-the-art static analysis-based techniques.
Finally, we discuss the main advantages and disadvantages of Timeloops as well
as other hardening techniques.

  In this paper, we analyze the performance of video streaming transcoding on
cloud VMs. Based on the analysis, we provide a model to quantify the degree of
suitability of each cloud VM type for various transcoding tasks. The provided
model can supply resource (VM) provisioning methods with accurate performance
and cost trade-offs to efficiently utilize cloud services for video streaming.
The model is then incorporated into a provably optimal scheduling method to
achieve the minimum possible transcoding finish time on heterogeneous cloud
VMs. The theoretical findings are validated through experiments on real cloud VM
types. The experiment results show that the model can accurately predict the

resolutions. The results also show that the proposed scheduling method can
effectively minimize the transcoding finish time on heterogeneous cloud VMs,

TESS have demonstrated that
planets are ubiquitous. However, the success of these missions heavily depends
on ground-based radial velocity (RV) surveys, which combined with transit
photometry can yield bulk densities and orbital properties. While most Kepler
host stars are too faint for detailed follow-up observations, TESS is detecting
planets orbiting nearby bright stars that are more amenable to RV
characterization. Here we introduce the TESS-Keck Survey (TKS), an RV program
using ~100 nights on Keck/HIRES to study exoplanets identified by TESS. The
primary survey aims are investigating the link between stellar properties and
the compositions of small planets; studying how the diversity of system
architectures depends on dynamical configurations or planet multiplicity;
identifying prime candidates for atmospheric studies with JWST; and
understanding the role of stellar evolution in shaping planetary systems. We
present a fully-automated target selection algorithm, which yielded 103 planets
in 86 systems for the final TKS sample. Most TKS hosts are inactive,
solar-like, main-sequence stars (4500 K < Teff < 6000 K) at a wide range of
metallicities. The selected TKS sample contains 71 small planets (Rp < 4 Re),
11 systems with multiple transiting candidates, 6 sub-day period planets and 3
planets in terrestrial systems with eccentric orbits. We look forward to
presenting the scientific findings from TKS.

Specifically, we investigate the emergence of communities of co-commenters,
that is, groups of users who often interact by commenting on the same posts and
may be driving the ongoing online discussions. In particular, we are interested
in salient co-interactions, i.e., interactions of co-commenters that occur more
often than expected by chance and under independent behavior. Unlike casual and
accidental co-interactions which normally happen in large volumes, salient
co-interactions are key elements driving the online discussions and,
ultimately, the information dissemination. We base our study on the analysis of
10 weeks of data centered around major elections in Brazil and Italy, following
both politicians and other celebrities. We extract and characterize the
communities of co-commenters in terms of topological structure, properties of
the discussions carried out by community members, and how some community
properties, notably community membership and topics, evolve over time. We show
that communities discussing political topics tend to be more engaged in the
debate by writing longer comments, using more emojis, and interacting with
other users more frequently. We also show that communities are characterized
by the topics that are being discussed and that some topics are more frequent
in certain communities. We argue that the structure of the discussion, with
groups of users discussing and possibly influencing each other, is fueled by
the emergence of communities of co-commenters. We draw our findings along a
theoretical framework that abstracts from the platform on which the discussion
takes place, making our insights applicable to other social media platforms.
Finally, we propose a set of measures that can help mitigating the spread of
misinformation, namely a filtering function that can be turned on by
authorities and that removes interactions that are likely to be driven by
accidental co-interactions.

We study the quantum annealing (QA) process for a collection of fully
entangled noisy qubits, comprised of two-dimensional bosonic oscillators,
analogous to a quantum harmonic oscillator network (HOON). We develop a
non-rigorous trial wavefunction that captures the important correlations in the
ground state of the quantum annealing process. This trial wavefunction is used
to estimate the success probability of finding the ground state in the
quantum-annealed ensemble. We study the behavior of this trial wavefunction for
a range of parameters and observe that it may be used to identify the
"macro-quantum" regime, where partial entanglement and partial decoherence may
be neglected. We show that the macro-quantum regime is characterized by a
threshold parameter threshold$\gamma_{th}$, such that for $\gamma <
\gamma_{th}$ the macro-quantum regime holds. Furthermore, we find that for
$\gamma \ll \gamma_{th}$ the overlap of the trial wavefunction with the
micro-canonical measure approaches unity. This may be used to study the
robustness of such a macro-quantum annealing process to decoherence.

  In this paper, we present a survey of requirements engineering in the gaming
industry. The survey begins with a characterization of the gaming industry,
discussing its relations with the market industry. This is followed by a
discussion of some challenges and best practices in the area of requirements
engineering in the gaming industry. Finally, we end with some research
directions and open problems in this area.
  In this article, we discuss the characterization of the gaming industry,
which has been missing from existing works on this topic. We discuss its
definition, unique aspects, and relations with other industries, including the
market industry. We also discuss some of the key concepts in the gaming industry
such as gaming genres, platforms, and the importance of intellectual property
rights. Finally, we discuss the characterization of a gaming industry from a
developing versus developed country perspective.

descent (DPSGD) is a fundamental challenge. Unlike the typical SGD, private
datasets cannot be used many times for hyperparameter search in DPSGD; e.g.,
via a grid search. Therefore, there is an essential need for algorithms that,
within a given search space, can find near-optimal hyperparameters for the best
achievable privacy-utility tradeoffs efficiently. We formulate this problem
into a general optimization framework for establishing a desirable
privacy-utility tradeoff, and systematically study three cost-effective
algorithms for being used in the proposed framework: evolutionary, Bayesian,
and reinforcement learning. Our experiments, for hyperparameter tuning in DPSGD
conducted on MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets, show that these three algorithms
significantly outperform the widely used grid search baseline. As this paper
offers a first-of-a-kind framework for hyperparameter tuning in DPSGD, we
discuss existing challenges and open directions for future studies. As we
believe our work has implications to be utilized in the pipeline of private
deep learning, we open-source our code at
https://github.com/AmanPriyanshu/DP-HyperparamTuning.
  I recommend reading Sections 1, 3, 4, 5, and 7 of this paper for a complete
understanding of the problem, the framework, and the results. Section 2 is a
comprehensive review of the related work and might be of interest to researchers
working in this area, but not necessary for the general reader.
  Many private machine learning algorithms assume access to multiple independent
samples from the private dataset. Differentially private stochastic gradient
descent (DPSGD) is one such strong assumption, and in this paper, we focus on
the problem of tuning hyperparameters in DPSGD. Unlike the typical SGD, private
datasets cannot be used many times for hyperparameter search in DPSGD; e.g.,
via a grid search. Therefore, there is an essential need for algorithms that,
within a given search space, can find near-optimal hyperparameters for the best
achievable privacy-utility tradeoffs efficiently.

world.In China, COVID-19 has caused severe consequences. Moreover, online
rumors during the COVID-19 pandemic increased people's panic about public
health and social stability. At present, understanding and curbing the spread
of online rumors is an urgent task. Therefore, we analyzed the rumor spreading
mechanism and propose a method to quantify a rumors' influence by the speed of
new insiders. The search frequency of the rumor is used as an observation
variable of new insiders. The peak coefficient and the attenuation coefficient
are calculated for the search frequency, which conforms to the exponential
distribution. We designed several rumor features and used the above two
coefficients as predictable labels. A 5-fold cross-validation experiment using
the mean square error (MSE) as the loss function showed that the recurrent
neural network (RNN) was Enhanced significantly by adding long short-term
memory (LSTM) and attention. In contrast, the graph neural network (GNN) had a
low test MSE. However, combining RNN and GNN could further improve the
predictive effect. Therefore, we propose a multi-task architecture that shares
features and combines RNN and GNN. This architecture's test MSE was reduced to
a minimum. Our work has two significant contributions. First, the search
frequency of online rumors generally conforms to an exponential distribution,
which is a fundamental mathematical theorem. Second, we conjecture that the
influence of rumors from search frequency is feasible in practice, and our
experiment's results with random and real data support this conjecture.
Finally, our study has applied value because it can help alleviate the spread
of rumors and reduce social risks.

their patients every day. Recently, there has been an increase in research
interest to subject this data to statistical analysis to gain more insights and
provide improved medical diagnoses. Such analyses require complex computations
on large volumes of data, demanding efficient data processing systems. This
paper shows that currently available data processing solutions either fail to
meet the performance requirements or lack simple and flexible programming
interfaces. To address this problem, we propose \emph{LifeStream}, a
high-performance stream processing engine for physiological data. LifeStream
hits the sweet spot between ease of programming by providing a rich temporal
query language support and performance by employing optimizations that exploit
the periodic nature of physiological data. We demonstrate that LifeStream
achieves end-to-end performance up to $7.5\times$ higher than state-of-the-art
streaming engines and $3.2\times$ than hand-optimized numerical libraries on
real-world datasets and workloads.
  We also show that LifeStream achieves 70% higher developer productivity
compared to popular big data processing engines, with minimal performance
trade-offs.
  Finally, LifeStream supports private statistical analyses by providing
efficient and secure multi-party computation protocols as a linearly composable
streaming operator. This allows domains such as healthcare to benefit from
data privacy and protection without sacrificing performance.
  In conclusion, LifeStream is a high-performance stream processing engine for
physiological data that achieves high performance, higher productivity, and
efficient private analyses.
  We believe that LifeStream's novel optimizations for periodic data and
flexible programming interface make it a strong candidate for efficiently
processing physiological data at scale.

neural network. Many loss functions have been designed to date, making a
correct choice nontrivial. However, elaborate justifications regarding the
choice of the loss function are not made in related work. This is, as we see
it, an indication of a dogmatic mindset in the deep learning community which
lacks empirical foundation. In this work, we consider deep neural networks in a
supervised classification setting and analyze the impact the choice of loss
function has onto the training result. While certain loss functions perform
suboptimally, our work empirically shows that under-represented losses such as
the KL Divergence can outperform the State-of-the-Art choices significantly,
highlighting the need to include the loss function as a tuned hyperparameter
rather than a fixed choice.
  We argue that the reason why the loss function is not considered a tuned
hyperparameter in related work is the non-competitive performance of neural
networks reported in our work when trained with a range of possible choices. To
illustrate this, we demonstrate how simple neural networks trained with the
right loss function can outperform state-of-the-art models both in terms of
classification accuracy and training efficiency (i.e., number of training
iterations needed to achieve a given accuracy). To facilitate easy comparison,
we conduct our experiments on well-studied datasets and report a set of standard
state-of-the-art models in addition to the ones mentioned above that can be
plugged in to improve performance.
  Finally, we propose a general algorithm called \textsc{FlexNet} that takes as
input a range of possible losses, and returns the best result among them. We
empirically show that \textsc{FlexNet} can outperform state-of-the-art models
significantly, verifying that the choice of loss function is crucial for the
training result.

  In the paper we present a stabilization strategy for the Navier-Stokes
equations which is an extension of R. Glowinski's work. One designs a linear
stabilizable boundary feedback controller which is oblique to boundary. The
main tool is a generalized Serrin's solution to non-homogeneous Navier-Stokes
equations, obtained by M. Su\'arez-Serrano. The strategy consists in having a
steady state solution to an related non-homogeneous Navier-Stokes equation,
which is a modified by adding a linear feedback term. The difference between the
non-homogeneous and homogeneous equations is a source term linear in the
velocity which, thanks to a persistence property, ensures the stability of the
solution. The linear feedback term added to the boundary feedback controller,
which is needed to have the desired behavior, is proved to be stabilizable.
Finally, we show the proof of existence of such a controller.

strain-induced crystallization in unfilled polymers. This phenomenon
significantly influences mechanical and thermal properties of polymers and has
to be taken into consideration when planning manufacturing processes as well as
applications of the final product. In order to simultaneously capture both
kinds of effects, the model proposed starts by introducing a triple
decomposition of the deformation gradient and furthermore uses thermodynamic
framework for material modeling based on the Coleman--Noll procedure and
minimum principle of the dissipation potential, which requires suitable
assumptions for the Helmholtz free energy and the dissipation potential. The
chosen setup yields evolution equations which are able to simulate the
formation and the degradation of crystalline regions accompanied by the
temperature change during a cyclic tensile test. The boundary value problem
corresponding to the described process includes the balance of linear momentum
and balance of energy and serves as a basis for the numerical implementation
within an FEM code. The~paper closes with the numerical examples showing the
microstructure evolution and temperature distribution for different material
samples.

demonstrations are difficult for the teacher to provide. For example in
robotics, providing kinesthetic demonstrations on a robotic manipulator
requires the teacher to control multiple degrees of freedom at once. The
difficulty of requiring optimal state action demonstrations limits the space of
problems where the teacher can provide quality feedback. As an alternative to
state action demonstrations, the teacher can provide corrective feedback such
as their preferences or rewards. Prior work has created algorithms designed to
learn from specific types of noisy feedback, but across teachers and tasks
different forms of feedback may be required. Instead we propose that in order
to learn from a diversity of scenarios we need to learn from a variety of
feedback. To learn from a variety of feedback we make the following insight:
the teacher's cost function is latent and we can model a stream of feedback as
a stream of loss functions. We then use any online learning algorithm to
minimize the sum of these losses. With this insight we can learn from a
diversity of feedback that is weakly correlated with the teacher's true cost

a quantum thermodynamics approach, by calculating two quintessential
thermodynamic quantities: the heat capacity and the quantum compressibility of
some model geometries filled with a quantum field at high and low temperatures.
This is because heat capacity at constant volume gives a measure of the
fluctuations of the energy density to the mean. When this ratio approaches or
exceeds unity, the validity of the canonical distribution is called into
question. Likewise, a system's compressibility at constant pressure is a
criterion for the validity of grand canonical ensemble. We derive the free
energy density and, from it, calculate the heat capacity and compressibility at
constant volume/presure for conformally coupled scalar fields in
anti-de Sitter and de Sitter spacetimes, as well as for massless fermions in
anti-de Sitter spacetime. Our main observation is that for all these models, in
the low temperature limit, the ratio of fluctuations to the mean is less than
unity, differently from what was found for conformally coupled scalar fields in
flat spacetime. This indicates that the issue of near-unity ratio of
fluctuations to mean in certain spacetimes is highly sensitive to the choice of
spacetime geometry.

correlators calculations, automatically incorporate the influence of the
spacetime curvature on the system's thermodynamics, since the latter is the
very purpose of considering non-flat geometries. Moreover, our approach is also
free from the ambiguities and uncertainties that are usually encountered in
defining stress-energy tensor in curved spacetime.

fluctuations to mean in certain spacetimes is still an open one and requires a
deeper investigation.

existence of a minimizer via minimization theory. Finally, we establish a
regularity result to the existence solution.

boundary value operator and the Navier inequality operator, the characterization
of harmonic functions in a domain with Navier boundary condition and the
compactness criterion for bounded subsets of Sobolev spaces. The existence proof
is based on the minimization theory and the invariance of the minimizer set
with respect to the Navier boundary value operator and the Navier inequality
operator. The regularity proof depends on the properties of the Navier boundary
value operator and the Navier inequality operator, the characterization of
harmonic functions in a domain with Navier boundary condition and the regularity
theorems for boundary value problems and elliptic equations.

classifier was selected for each drug. The quality of classification was
surprisingly high with sensitivity and specificity (evaluated by leave-one-out
cross-validation) being greater than 70\% for almost all classification tasks.

achieved for cannabis, crack, ecstasy, legal highs, LSD, and volatile substance

adversary cannot create two ciphertexts both of which decrypt to the same

disadvantage that they either guarantee one-time security (that is, the
encryption key can only be used once to encrypt the message) in the plain model
or they guaranteed security in the random oracle model. We construct unclonable
encryption schemes with semantic security. We present two constructions (for
public-key and private-key settings) from minimal cryptographic assumptions.

information-theoretic one-time secure construction of Broadbent and Lord. The
success probability of the adversary in their construction was guaranteed to be
$0.85^n$, where $n$ is the length of the message. It was interesting to
understand whether the ideal success probability of (negligibly close to)
$0.5^n$ was unattainable. We generalize their construction to be based on a
broader class of monogamy of entanglement games. We demonstrate a simple

schemes that attempt to formalize the intuitive idea of, "binding" the message

Broadbent and Lord's constructions.

driven by line-scattering of the star's radiative momentum, while in the Sun

interactions on an event-by-event basis and will provide valuable data for

Laboratory (LANL) in both 2019 and 2020, with neutron energies between 0 and

generation, imitation learning has been viewed as a vital direction in the
context of robot skill learning. In contrast to unconstrained imitation
learning which ignores possible internal and external constraints arising from
environments and robot kinematics/dynamics, recent works on constrained
imitation learning allow for transferring human skills to unstructured
scenarios, further enlarging the application domain of imitation learning.
While various constraints have been studied, e.g., joint limits, obstacle
avoidance and plane constraints, the problem of nonlinear hard constraints has
not been well-addressed. In this paper, we propose extended kernelized movement
primitives (EKMP) to cope with most of the key problems in imitation learning,
including nonlinear hard constraints. Specifically, EKMP is capable of learning
the probabilistic features of multiple demonstrations, adapting the learned
skills towards arbitrary desired points in terms of joint position and
velocity, avoiding obstacles at the level of robot links, as well as satisfying
arbitrary linear and nonlinear, equality and inequality hard constraints.
Besides, the connections between EKMP and state-of-the-art motion planning
approaches are discussed. Several evaluations including the planning of joint
trajectories for a 7-DoF robotic arm are provided to verify the effectiveness
of our framework.

conductors with antisymmetric spin-orbit
coupling in a Zeeman magnetic field provide a promising route to realize
superconducting states with non-Abelian topological order and therefore
fault-tolerant quantum computation. Here we use a quantum Monte Carlo dynamical
cluster approximation to study the superconducting properties of a doped
two-dimensional attractive Hubbard model with Rashba spin-orbit coupling in a
Zeeman magnetic field. We generally find that the Rashba coupling has a
beneficial effect towards s-wave superconductivity. In the presence of a finite
Zeeman field, when superconductivity is suppressed by Pauli pair-breaking, the
Rashba coupling counteracts the spin imbalance created by the Zeeman field by
mixing the spins, and thus restores superconductivity at finite temperatures.
We show that this favorable effect of the spin-orbit coupling is traced to a
spin-flip driven enhancement of the amplitude for the propagation of a pair of
electrons in time-reversed states. Moreover, by inspecting the Fermi surface of
the interacting model, we show that for sufficiently large Rashba coupling and
Zeeman field, the superconducting state is expected to be topologically
non-trivial.
  Our results suggest that by tuning the Rashba coupling one may in experiments
manage the appearance of a fully gapped superconducting state, a prerequisite
for any application of superconducting quantum computation.
  Finally, our work provides an empirical rule-of-thumb for assessing the
importance of spin-orbit coupling in leading to superconductivity in
disordered systems.
  We also compare our results to a mean-field theory and provide a
justification for its validity in the presence of a Zeeman field.
  This work is an extension of our previous study [Phys. Rev. Lett. 128, 077001
(2022)] where we considered a related model with repulsive Hubbard interaction
and showed that the Rashba coupling helps to drive an $s+x$ superconducting
state. Here we show that in doped attractive Hubbard models, $s+x$ is not the
only possible mixture of superconducting pair-functions, and that the model
also develops $s+y$ symmetry.

identify a new transition in the vortex lattice state of
La$_{2-x}$Sr$_{x}$CuO$_4$ (LSCO). The transition, observed in magnetic fields
exceeding 35 T and temperatures far below zero field $T_c$, is detected in the

rotation of the vortex lattice in a $d$-wave superconductor. The doping level of
$p=0.17$ falls on the slope of the van Hove singularity, in agreement with
theoretical predictions for LSCO [1]. The location of the transition in the
magnetic field vs. temperature plane is also in agreement with theoretical
predictions for a $d$-wave superconductor [2].
  The origin of the $d$-wave symmetry of the order parameter in LSCO is not
obvious, but if true, the 45 degrees rotation of the vortex lattice should be
a generic feature of $d$-wave superconductors. The lack of this transition in
other materials could indicate a more $s$-wave like symmetry of the order

for discovering wide separation binary asteroids in wide field surveys. We then
applied these techniques to images of main belt asteroids in the 4 to 60 km
size range captured by Pan-STARRS1. Johnston (2019) lists fewer than 10 known
binaries in this size range with separations greater than 10% of the primary's

understanding the limits of binary stability and improving our knowledge of
asteroid masses. We analyzed each image by: i) comparing the major axis
orientation of the asteroid's elliptical PSF to its non-sidereal rate on the
sky, and ii) comparing the one-dimensional median profile created by collapsing
the image along the asteroid's direction of motion to that of nearby field
stars. For both methods, we flagged any results that deviated significantly
from the expected measurements of single asteroids, and those targets with the
most flags were identified as binary candidates for confirmation with
high-acuity imaging.

and that they were most useful for asteroids of 20-40 km in size. We also found
that the pairing function of binaries discovered by this technique was
consistent with random spin-orbit misalignments. Upon further investigation, we
found that this was likely due to our sample being dominated by asteroids in

tools for visualization and analysis of
next-generation sequencing datasets. BigBeams is a web-based framework for
visualization of genomic substitution maps generated by the BiblioMaps
algorithm. Genomic regions of the genome that are under the influence of the
same regulatory element can be visualized as a group, with a common "beam"
label. The position and extent of these regions can be adjusted dynamically
based on the genomic coordinate scale. The appearance of the genomic regions
and the beam labels can be customized in real-time. The framework also allows
the visualization of multiple substitution maps generated from different
species or under different conditions, with the option of adjusting the
transparency of each map for comparative analysis. BigCapture is a web tool
for visualization of genomic regions surrounding Gene Venoms (GVs) and
Genomic Loci (GLs) in different species, with customizable genomic interval
colors. BigMotif is a web tool for visualization of a set of inter-related
short-range genomic substitution maps generated from mapping of nucleotide
variability (SNPs, k-mers) or structural variability (indels). BigMotif
provides a framework for visualization of multiple motif maps in a single
image with customizable colors, with the option of adjusting the transparency
of each motif map for comparative analysis. BigAnnot is a web tool for
visualization of genomic regions surrounding a set of selected genomic
features (GVs, GLs, repeat regions, snps, indels, k-mers, fusions, and
chimeric transcripts). BigAnnot provides a customizable interface allowing the
selection of a set of genomic features of interest and their visualization
along the genomic coordinate scale.
  BigBeams, BigCapture, BigMotif, and BigAnnot are implemented in Python with
the use of Flask as the web framework, Bootstrap for the front-end development
and Plotly for the interactive visualization. The tools are designed to be
modular, with the use of separate databases for each tool, making the
reorganization of the database structure possible with minimal disruption to
the functioning of the other tools.

Jurassic-Cretaceous intraplate rift zone between the African and South American
plates during the final breakup of western Gondwana. By quantitatively
accounting for crustal deformation in the Central and West African and
South American rift zones, we construct a kinematic model of pre-breakup
rifting in the West African and South Atlantic basins. Our model suggests that
the Central and West African rift zones experienced total extensional strains
of similar values, which were however accommodated at different rates. The
greater extensional strain rate in the Central African rift zone is believed
to have caused its earlier magmatic rift initiation compared to the West African
rift zone. Final breakup boundary changes between South America and Africa,
documented from Late Cretaceous to Palaeogene, are best explained by a
persistent polycyclic motion of the South American plate along a SW-trending
axis during the final breakup of western Gondwana. Our model indicates that
the conjugate West African and South Atlantic margins were formed as a common
rifting system, with the Atlantic margin representing only the portion that
separated between South America and Africa after the final breakup of western
Gondwana.
  The origin of the pre-breakup continental configuration of western Gondwana
remains controversial. By accounting for crustal deformation in the Central and
West African and South American rift zones during the final breakup of western
Gondwana, we propose a new conceptual model of its final breakup kinematics.
Accounting for geochronological, geochemical, paleomagnetic and basin
structural data from the conjugate margins, our model suggests that the Central
and West African rift zones evolved as branch of a large intraplate rift zone
that separated Africa from South America during the final breakup of western
Gondwana. By quantitatively accounting for crustal deformation in the Central and
West African and South American rift zones, our model indicates that the
final breakup boundary between South America and Africa was likely formed as
the result of a continued polycyclic motion of the South American plate along
a SW-trending axis, which started at least since the Late Cretaceous. Before
that the combined Central and West African rift zones likely separated from

interactions. Specifically, we choose Dungeons and Dragons (D&D) -- a
role-playing game consisting of multiple player characters and a Dungeon Master
(DM) who collaborate to achieve a set of goals that are beneficial to the
players -- as a testbed for this task. Here, each of the player characters is a
student, with their own personas and abilities, and the DM is the teacher, an
arbitrator of the rules of the world and responsible for assisting and guiding
the students towards a global goal. We propose a theory-of-mind-inspired
methodology for training such a DM with reinforcement learning (RL), where a
DM: (1) learns to predict how the players will react to its utterances using a
dataset of D&D dialogue transcripts; and (2) uses this prediction as a reward
function providing feedback on how effective these utterances are at guiding
the players towards a goal. Human and automated evaluations show that a DM
trained with RL to generate guidance by incorporating a theory-of-mind of the
players significantly improves the players' ability to achieve goals grounded
in their shared world.
  We also observe interesting properties of such a DM, including that the
theory-of-mind of the players can be used to improve the DM's overall
communicative effectiveness and that the DM's theory-of-mind can be learned in
an end-to-end manner using RL. Finally, we find that adding theory-of-mind to
a DM provides natural mechanisms for improving the fairness of the D&D game,
leading to more successful collaborations between the DM and players.
  Overall, the G4C dataset and theory-of-mind-inspired methodology present a
new paradigm for grounded, multi-agent tasks and show how such a paradigm can
be used to study important social concepts like cooperation and fairness.

process is an open and challenging question in biology. Recent studies classify
the topology and geometry of knotted proteins by analysing the distribution of
a protein's planar projections using topological objects called knotoids. We
approach the analysis of proteins with the same topology by introducing a
topologically inspired statistical metric between their knotoid distributions.
We detect geometric differences between trefoil proteins by characterising
their entanglement and we recover a clustering by sequence similarity. By
looking directly at the geometry and topology of their native states, we are
able to probe different folding pathways for proteins forming open-ended
trefoil knots. Interestingly, our pipeline reveals that the folding pathway of
shallow knotted Carbonic Anhydrases involves the creation of a double-looped
structure, differently from what was previously observed for deeply knotted
trefoil proteins. We validate this with Molecular Dynamics simulations.
Moreover, we find that trefoil proteins have higher flexibility and a larger
binding surface compared to non-knotted and cylindrical proteins. This work
shows that proteins with the same trefoil topology can have vastly different
geometries, and that knotting introduces localized flexibility regions.
Additionally, our approach suggests that knotting may enhance the binding
efficiency of enzymes by providing more binding surfaces.
  Finally, we question whether the prevalence of trefoil knots in nature is
due to accidental topology or if it is instead the result of an underlying
biological benefit, by building a statistical mechanical model of protein
formation. Our results show that trefoil topology is favoured with respect to
cylindrical topology at high energies (temperatures). This work shows that even
a simple model can capture the prevalence of trefoil knots if energy (stability)
is an important factor in the folding process.
  In conclusion, this work investigates the folding pathways of knotted
proteins from a geometric and topological perspective, and demonstrates that
knotting can lead to localized flexibility and binding enhancement.
Moreover, it shows that the prevalence of trefoil knots in nature can be
explained by the proteins' stability to high temperatures.

energy (EDE), is a proposed solution to the Hubble tension. Currently, there is
no consensus in the literature as to whether EDE can simultaneously solve the
Hubble tension and provide an adequate fit to the data from the cosmic
microwave background (CMB) and large-scale structure of the universe. In this
work, we deconstruct the current constraints from the Planck CMB and the
full-shape clustering data of the Baryon Oscillation Spectroscopic Survey
(BOSS) to understand the origin of different conclusions in the literature. We
use two different analyses, a grid sampling and a profile likelihood, to
investigate whether the current constraints suffer from volume effects upon
marginalization and are biased towards some values of the EDE fraction,
$f_\mathrm{EDE}$. We find that $f_\mathrm{EDE}$ allowed by the data strongly
depends on the particular choice of the other parameters of the model and that
several choices of these parameters prefer larger values of $f_\mathrm{EDE}$
than in our main analysis. This suggests that volume effects are the reason
behind the disagreement in the literature. Motivated by this, we propose a
method to correctly compute the EDE profile likelihood and select a set of
parameters of interest that is robust to changes in the other parameters of
the model. Our main observation is that the EDE profile likelihood is strongly
affected by the choice of the primordial power spectrum parameters, which is
not mandatory to model EDE. We show that by fixing these parameters to their
best-fitting values from the Planck data, the EDE model receives no tension
from the CMB and LSS data, and can only shift the present Hubble parameter by
$\sim 0.6 \sigma$, an insufficient solution to the Hubble tension. However,
when allowing some variation in these parameters, we find that $f_\mathrm{EDE}$
can take values between $0$ and $10\%$ depending on the choice of the other
parameters. We discuss our results and conclude that EDE is not a robust model
for the Hubble tension, and other solutions that can consistently model the
CMB and LSS data should be considered.

scale and diversity if crowdsourced and is computationally expensive to extend

This problem studies the model where the same sequence from some set is
transmitted over multiple channels, and the decoder receives the different
outputs. Assume that the transmitted sequence is at distance $d$ from some code
and there are at most $r$ errors in every channel. Then the sequence
reconstruction problem is to find the minimum number of channels required to
recover exactly the transmitted sequence that has to be greater than the
maximum intersection between two metric balls of radius $r$, where the distance
between their centers is at least $d$. In this paper, we study the sequence
reconstruction problem of permutations under the Hamming distance. In this
model, we define a Cayley graph and find the exact value of the largest
intersection of two metric balls in this graph under the Hamming distance for
$r=4$ with $d=2r$, and for $r=5$ with $d=2r-1$. For other values of $r$ and
$d$, we give lower and upper bounds for the largest intersection of two metric
balls. These bounds are close to each other for small values of $r$ and large
values of $d$.
  We also study the sequence reconstruction problem of permutations under the
Hamming distance when the number of channels is limited. In this model, we find
the minimum number of transmitted sequences that are required to achieve the
desired recovery performance for any transmitted sequence. For this, we define
a graph and find the minimum number of vertices with degree at least $\delta$
in a graph under certain conditions. These results are also applicable to the
fault-tolerant sequence reconstruction problem, where we want to recover the
transmitted sequence when there are at most $r_1$ errors in every channel and
also when we are given at most $r_2$ errors among the received outputs.

problem. We define a polar code as follows: first, we find the required number

necessary number of layers to recover exactly the transmitted sequence
fault-tolerantly, and finally we construct a polar code of length
$2^{n_1}\cdot2^{n_2}$ with these two numbers.

Each question is written by an NLP practitioner who read only the title and

practitioners who also provide supporting evidence to answers. We find that
existing models that do well on other QA tasks do not perform well on answering

space available to any pair of primers (i.e., partition) is virtually
unlimited. We expose and leverage the flexibility with which this address space
can be managed to provide rich and functional storage semantics, such as
hierarchical data organization and efficient and flexible implementations of
data updates. Furthermore, to leverage the full power of the prefix-based
nature of PCR addressing, we define a methodology for transforming an arbitrary
indexing scheme into a PCR-compatible equivalent. This allows us to run PCR
with primers that can be variably extended to include a desired part of the
index, and thus narrow down the scope of the reaction to retrieve a specific
object (e.g., file or directory) within the partition with high precision. Our
wetlab evaluation demonstrates the practicality of the proposed ideas and shows
140x reduction in sequencing cost retrieval of smaller objects within the
partition.

simulation benchmarks that model both internal partition management and the
process of mapping PCR products to targets. The results show that our approaches
yield significant reductions in the time of data updates as well as the time of
map detection, especially for smaller objects and smaller scales. The map
detection benefit is due to the tags we attach to the PCR products to facilitate

effectiveness of our approaches is mainly due to the high fidelity of PCR and the
low error-rate of map detection that they enable.

flexible storage semantics we can significantly improve the usability of DNA

(SWEs) are commonly used for this purpose. However, traditional numerical

riverbed profile measurement (bathymetry). In this work, we propose a two-stage
process in which, first, using the principal component geostatistical approach

velocity measurements, and then use machine learning (ML) algorithms to obtain
a fast solver for the SWEs. The fast solver uses realizations from the
posterior bathymetry distribution and takes as input the prescribed range of
BCs. The first stage allows us to predict flow velocities without direct
measurement of the bathymetry. Furthermore, we augment the bathymetry posterior
distribution to a more general class of distributions before providing them as
inputs to ML algorithm in the second stage. This allows the solver to
incorporate future direct bathymetry measurements into the flow velocity
prediction for improved accuracy, even if the bathymetry changes over time
compared to its original indirect estimation. We propose and benchmark three
different solvers, referred to as PCA-DNN (principal component analysis-deep
neural network), SE (supervised encoder), and SVE (supervised variational
encoder), for predicting the SWEs for given post-bathymetry densities. The
results show that the SVE solver is more than 100 times faster than traditional
numerical solvers while preserving excellent accuracy (error less than 10% in
flow velocity prediction) for a wide range of bathymetry values. The results

prediction accuracy for flow velocities (error less than 5%) even when the
bathymetry changes from its original indirectly estimated value. We believe that

problems for predicting river flow velocities.

  A novel characterization of a digital camera is introduced in terms of the
camera characteristic function that describes the mapping of the global
illumination of an image to its pixel intensity. Based on this function, a
method for selecting the exposure settings of a bracket of images is
introduced. The main idea is to select the exposure settings such that the
intensity difference between any two images due to the camera characteristic
function is at least a predetermined minimum difference. This allows for
removing shadows or highlights from an image by fusing two appropriate images
from the bracket. In addition, a method for fusion of a bracket of images is
introduced. The main idea is to minimize a least squares fitting criterion
subject to the constraint of intensity difference between any two images. This
formulation allows for weighting the images to be fused in addition to
removing shadows or highlights. Both of these methods are implemented on a
smartphone platform and comparison results with several existing methods are
presented indicating the effectiveness as well as the computational efficiency
of the introduced solution.

field of machine learning. With CDL, researchers aim to structure and encode
causal knowledge in the extremely flexible representation space of deep
learning models. Doing so will lead to more informed, robust, and general
predictions and inference -- which is important! However, CDL is still in its
infancy. With the large variety of different approaches, it is difficult to
compare and establish sound conclusions. In this survey, we take a step back
and establish a formal framework that includes many of the approaches that are
needed for CDL. Within this framework, we discuss confounding, direct and
indirect effects, path-specific effects, and mode-based representations. We
compare and contrast several recent models that encode these different
quantities and need them all to encode the full causal capability of a model.
Finally, we discuss some important open research questions in CDL and provide
a user-stored dataset of experiments to facilitate further research.

gradient masking is
amongst proposed adversarial defenses. Defenses that rely on this phenomenon
are considered failed, and can easily be broken. Despite this, there has been
little investigation into ways of measuring the phenomenon of gradient masking
and enabling comparisons of its extent amongst different networks. In this
work, we investigate gradient masking under the lens of its mensurability,
departing from the idea that it is a binary phenomenon. We propose and motivate
several metrics for it, performing extensive empirical tests on defenses
suspected of exhibiting different degrees of gradient masking. These are
computationally cheaper than strong attacks, enable comparisons between models,
and do not require the large time investment of tailor-made attacks for
specific models. Our results reveal metrics that are successful in measuring
the extent of gradient masking across different networks
(https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.12141). We also demonstrate that rich insights can
be gained from their output, without the need for expensive strong testing. We
report findings on a large set of models and defenses, and demonstrate how the
results can be used to improve attacks and evaluate the performance of
state-of-the-art networks.
  We study the notion of gradient masking, a phenomenon first introduced to
adversarial training. We propose and motivate several metrics to measure its
extent, tailorable to the specific context of our investigations. Our work
departing from the idea that gradient masking is a binary phenomenon, has been
extensively tested on several networks defending against adversarial
attacks. Comparisons enabled by our metrics have yielded interesting insights
into how different interventions (e.g. data augmentations, architecture
variations) relate to gradient masking. Crucially, our metrics have been
designed to be cheaper than strong testing, and have therefore enabled a rich
dataset of observations. We have also noticed interesting variations in the
extent of gradient masking across different networks, which has enabled us to
filter out models whose analysis is not meaningful. This has been particularly
useful when investigating the effect of adversarially training a network. In
the context of our investigation, we have also noticed that a small set of
interventions are able to induce a large degree of gradient masking for a cost of
little to no benefit. We argue that the small benefit seen is not worth the cost
of the loss of generalizability. Indeed our metrics have shown that models
trained with higher degrees of gradient masking tend to generalize less.

an overview of the relationship between
Hodge-theoretic and geometric compactifications of moduli spaces of algebraic
varieties.
  Let $\mathcal{M}$ be the moduli space of algebraic varieties of some kind,
equipped with a natural Hodge metric induced by its universal family
$\pi:\mathcal{V}\to\mathcal{M}$. A Hodge-theoretic compactification of
$\mathcal{M}$ is, by definition, a compactification $\overline{\mathcal{M}}$
induced by the K\"ahler-Einstein metric on $\mathcal{V}$ (which exists, by
work of Tian and others, in many interesting cases). On the other hand, a
geometric compactification of $\mathcal{M}$ is obtained by attaching to
$\mathcal{M}$ some classifying spaces for the stabiliser groups of points in
$\mathcal{V}$, using the fact that $\pi_{\ast}(\mathcal{V}/\Delta)\sim
\mathbb{H}^{*}(\Delta, \mathbb{Z})$ for suitable subvarieties $\Delta\subset
\mathcal{V}$. We survey the relationship between these two approaches, focusing
on cases where they coincide up to proper disjoint union of strata. We also
illustrate the difference between them in other cases, where the geometry of
the geometric compactification does not carry information about the
Hodge-theoretic compactification.
  Finally, we propose a conjectural framework linking these ideas to other
work in moduli space, algebraic cycles and motivic cohomology.
  We hope that this note will be useful to both Hodge theorists and geometers
working on moduli spaces.
  It should be clear that our point of view is strongly influenced by our
interest in Hodge theory of moduli spaces and its applications, and there are
many other interesting perspectives on compactifications of moduli spaces that
we do not address at all.

separatrix surface that separates two different types of oscillations. A large
amplitude oscillation is initiated if a trajectory moves from the "inner" to
the "outer side" of this surface. A set of conditions on the normal form
variables are obtained to determine whether a trajectory would exhibit another

which measures the disorder in the time to a regime shift. We find that for a
low density of holes, the disorder is maximum at a certain distance from the

state, beyond which a macroscopic fraction of trajectories experience a
regime shift at the same time. This happens when the probability of observing a
trajectory that exhibits one MMO orbit before a regime shift is of the order of
the inverse hole density. A critical density of holes is found analytically,
and numerically verified through direct simulation of the model.

recognition in the dark.
In this work, we present our results on the ARID dataset. Most previous works
only evaluate performance on large, well illuminated datasets like Kinetics and
HMDB51. We demonstrate that our work is able to achieve a very low error rate
while being trained on a much smaller dataset of dark videos. We also explore a
variety of training and inference strategies including domain transfer
methodologies and also propose a simple but useful frame selection strategy.
Our empirical results demonstrate that we beat previously published baseline
models by 11%.
  We also demonstrate that our work is able to generalize to a variety of
real-world settings. First, we show that our model is able to recognize actions
in dark videos taken by unstructured consumer cameras. Second, we demonstrate
that our model is able to recognize actions even when the lighting conditions
vary greatly across training and test videos. Finally, we also show that our model
is able to recognize human actions from surveillance videos.
  We also explore a variety of supervision scenarios. First, we study the
supervision required to achieve a decent error rate. We find that a small
annotation corpus annotated with high inter rater agreement is able to yield
good results. We also study the impact of labeling a small set of frames per
video. We find that frame level annotations are able to significantly improve
error rates especially for videos with low luminosity.
  Additionally, we also explore a variety of simple but useful frame selection
strategies. We find that a variety of simple strategies are able to significantly
improve error rates especially for videos with low luminosity. We also find that
models that select frames automatically yield lower error rates compared to
models that use all frames.
  Finally, we also study the impact of multimodality. We create a dataset of 2
min video clips annotated with action labels and keypoint annotations. We find
that using both visual and skeletal information is able to significantly improve
error rates.
  We also demonstrate a variety of interesting application demos including a
surveillance system and a ranking system for recommended videos.
  Overall, our results and experiments demonstrate that supervised action
recognition in the dark is a promising research problem with a variety of
interesting questions and also a range of novel applications.

compact star-bursting cores with properties consistent with forming galaxy

lopsided. Therefore, `outside-in' quenching is ongoing in the three group
galaxies. We propose an overall scenario in which the strong mass lopsidedness
in the disks (ranging from factors of 1.6 to $>$3), likely generated under the
effects of accreted gas and clumps, is responsible for their star-formation
suppression, while funnelling gas into the nuclei and thus creating the central
starbursts. The lopsided side of the disks marks the location of accretion
streams impact, with additional matter components (dust and stars) detected in
their close proximity directly tracing the inflow direction. The interaction
with the accreted clumps, which can be regarded as minor-mergers, leads the
major axes of the three galaxies to be closely aligned with the outer
Lyman-$\alpha$-emitting accretion nebulae and with the overall shape of the
interacting IGM within the group, as derived from our observations and from the
recent one by the MUSE consortium. The observed properties of the group galaxies
and their surroundings are consistent with the idea that they are on the crossroad
of further accretion and possible mergers with other systems still unseen.

galaxies and its link to minor mergers with clumps suggests that such a physical
process might be the driver of their inside-out quenching.

rotation profiles in giant stars may be a proof function of the presence of a
planetary system around the star.

ophysical computational model of brain
regions relevant to Parkinson's Disease based on local field potential data
collected from the brain of marmoset monkeys. Parkinson's disease is a
neurodegenerative disorder, linked to the death of dopaminergic neurons at the
substantia nigra pars compacta, which affects the normal dynamics of the basal
ganglia-thalamus-cortex neuronal circuit of the brain. Although there are
multiple mechanisms that have been proposed to explain the disease, a full
understanding of the neurophysiological mechanisms responsible for the motor
symptoms of Parkinson's disease is still lacking. Mathematical and computational
models have been developed to understand the disease, but there are still
number of issues, such as the interpretation of the reference parameters, that
prevent the models to reach a statistical population level and to be interpreted
in the context of a real disease. To address these issues, we propose a
multi-population model that includes five coupled differential equations
representing the differential average dynamics of five brain regions: the
substantia Nigra (SN), the Globus Pallidus Internus (GPI), the Globus Pallidus
Exterus (GPE), the Thalamus (THA) and the Primary Motor Cortex (MCC). Our
biophysical model is aimed at representing the average changes induced by
Parkinson's disease in the normal dynamics of the basal ganglia-thalamus-cortex
neuronal circuit and to test in a computational environment a pharmacological
intervention (L-DOPA treatment) that is known to provide benefits to patients.
Results from the model provide an understanding of how the death of nigral
dopaminergic neurons affects normal motor processing and how L-DOPA treatment
induces normalisation of the model's features. The approach presented here offers
an opportunity to re-examine neurodegeneration and neuronal replacement
processes in PD, and to test the effectiveness of L-DOPA treatment in
computational environments representing a real disease.
  The model is available as a C++ executable file, and as a corresponding R
package ("R6 version"), available from GitHub, where all the parameters and
variables used are described in a commented text file. The models is also
available in a simplified version using the Neuronal Dynamics platform of
9DegreesEast. This work is a contribution to the ultimate goal of understanding
the mechanisms of movement in health and in Parkinson's disease

attractive framework as it is fundamentally dynamical, removing some of the
assumptions of mass-flux convection schemes which are invalid at current model
resolutions. However, it is still not understood how best to close the
multi-fluid equations for atmospheric convection. In this paper we develop a
simple two-fluid, single-column model with one rising and one falling fluid. No

the correct scaling of the heat flux (Nu) is predicted over six orders of

structures of convection.

fundamental response of the model to changes in control variables, essentially

parameterisations, including convection.

sum of all the other closures and sources of error in the model. We estimate
that for typical meteorological scales (10-100m) the closures may be of order

CMS) detector is one of two general-purpose
detectors that measure the products of high energy particle interactions in the
Large Hadron Collider (LHC) at CERN. The silicon pixel detector is the
innermost component of the CMS tracking system. The detector which was in
operation between 2009 and 2016 has now been replaced with an upgraded one in
the beginning of 2017. During the previous shutdown period of the LHC, a
prototype readout system and a third disk was inserted into the old forward
pixel detector with eight prototype blades constructed using the new digital
read-out chips. Testing the performance of these pilot modules enabled us to
gain operational experience with the upgraded detector. In this paper, the
reconstruction and analysis of the data taken with the new modules are
presented including information on the calibration of the reconstruction
software. The hit finding efficiency and track-hit residual distributions are
also shown.
  Based on 4 pb$^{-1}$ of data taken in 2015 with the insertions in place,
the hit finding efficiency is about 98.5% with a small dependence on track
direction and momentum. Good alignment of the pixels with the CMS magnetic
field is shown, with residuals improving with increasing track momentum. At
high momentum above 100 GeV, they approach the design value of less than 8
mm.
  Measurement of the hit residual distribution has shown that the precision
approaches the design value of less than 1.5 mm at all radii, with the
largest contribution to the residuals coming from the track reconstruction
rather than the pixel detector mechanics or electronics.
  Finally, with all hits correctly identified and measured, the impact on
physics performance such as jet reconstruction and particle-flow
reconstruction is also presented.
  In addition, examples of physics results such as Higgs boson and diboson
measurements are shown.
  The experience gained from the operational use of the pilot modules has been
extensive and has prepared the operation of the new generation CMS pixel
detector.

treatments are often evaluated by analyzing the average treatment effects and
risks. The stochastic efficiency with respect to a function is often employed
in such evaluations through ranking the certainty equivalents of each
treatment. The main challenge of using this method is gathering an adequate
number of observations to produce results with statistical power. However, in
many cases, only a limited number of trials are replicated in field
experiments, leaving an inadequate number of observations. In addition, this
method focuses only on the farmer's profit without incorporating the impact of
disease pressure on yield and profit. The objective of our study is to propose
a methodology to address the issue of an insufficient number of observations
using simulations and take into account the effect of disease pressure on yield
through a quantile regression model. We apply this method to the case of
strawberry disease management in Florida.

profits from the current pesticide treatments and that the best treatment is
not the same at different levels of disease pressure. Without considering
disease pressure, the pesticide treatments can be efficiently ranked; however,
the rankings can change with increasing disease pressure. Farmers who grow
strawberries in other regions and climates can benefit from this study by
understanding how disease pressure affects yield and profit, and by learning
about the efficacy of different pesticide treatments.

  The frog model is a type of random walk on a graph, where multiple frogs
start at the root and jump to independent random neighbors until only one frog
remains. In this work, we study the simplest case of the frog model, where
each jump is to one of two possible neighbors. We show that the frog model on
a tree with nonuniform edge probabilities is equivalent to a product measure
on the set of paths of the walk, whose density of zeros is exponentially
bounded. This allows us to compute the expectation of a wide class of
observables, including the size distribution of the set of sites occupied by
the frogs. We argue that the model is in a high-temperature phase if this
distribution is roughly exponential, and in a low-temperature phase if it is
roughly power-law. In the case of a uniformly generated tree, we prove
exactly that the transition from exponential to power-law occurs at a frog
density of order the degree of the tree.

other vertices, while the opposite frog stands still. We characterize the
equilibrium measure as the product measure on the vertices of the tree, with
a certain i.i.d. nonnegative weights. This equilibrium measure is doubly
convex, and its largest convex majorant can be explicitly described. We
construct a random walk on the vertices of the tree, whose equilibrium
probability is approximately equal to the largest convex minorant of the
equilibrium measure, if the degree of the tree is large compared to the
number of frogs per site. This allows us to study the asymptotic behavior of
the monotone frog model via the study of a related walk on the tree.

expensive or even impossible. To overcome this challenge, in this paper, we
propose a novel learning framework called Co-Imitation Learning (CoIL) to
exploit the past good experiences of the agents themselves without expert
demonstration. Specifically, we train two different agents via letting each of
them alternately explore the environment and exploit the peer agent's

visits to news sources aligned with their own political leaning are
substantially longer than their visits to other news sources. Next, we show

as evidenced by the emergence of clear partisan communities of news domains
from aggregated browsing patterns. Finally, we tackle the important question of
the role of user choices in polarization. Are users simply following the links
proffered by their Web environment, or do they exacerbate partisan polarization
by intentionally pursuing like-minded news sources? To answer this question, we
compare browsing patterns with the underlying hyperlink structure spanned by

scenario wherein the heterogeneity in browsing habits across users leads to

partisan polarization is exacerbated by the fact that users are more likely to
visit other users' favorite news sources. In particular, we show that such
interactions can lead to the emergence of strong polarized communities along

that evaluates each finite word over A_p={0,1,...,p-1} to some rational number.
We let N_p/q denote the image of this evaluation function. In particular, N_p/q
contains all nonnegative integers and the literature on base p/q usually
focuses on the set of words that are evaluated to nonnegative integers; it is a
rather chaotic language which is not context-free. On the contrary, we study
here the subsets of (N_p/q)^d that are p/q-recognisable, i.e. realised by
finite automata over (A_p)^d. First, we give a characterisation of these sets
as those definable in a first-order logic, similar to the one given by the
B\"uchi-Bruy\`ere Theorem for integer bases numeration systems. Second, we show
that the natural order relation and the modulo-q operator are not
p/q-recognisable.
  We also give some sufficient conditions for a subset of (N_p/q)^d to be
p/q-recognisable, and we show by a construction that every p/q-recognisable
set is effectively definable in this logic. Finally, we give an example of a
relatively simple automaton and we show that the set it defines is very close
to the set of words that are evaluated to integers; we conjecture that it realises the largest possible p/q-recognisable set.
  All these results show that while contrastingly to integer bases
numeration systems, there is no nice structural result characterising
p/q-recognisable sets, the study of base p/q allows us to construct counterexamples and to
illustrate the complexity of rational bases numeration systems.

Edges and boundaries encode shape information, while textures manifest the
appearance of regions. Despite the success of Convolutional Neural Networks
(CNNs) in computer vision and medical image analysis applications,
predominantly only texture abstractions are learned, which often leads to
imprecise boundary delineations. In medical imaging, expert manual segmentation
often relies on organ boundaries; for example, to manually segment a liver, a
medical practitioner usually identifies edges first and subsequently fills in
the segmentation mask. Motivated by these observations, we propose a
plug-and-play module, dubbed Edge-Gated CNNs (EG-CNNs), that can be used with
existing encoder-decoder architectures to process both edge and texture
information. The EG-CNN learns to emphasize the edges in the encoder, to
predict crisp boundaries by an auxiliary edge supervision, and to fuse its
output with the original CNN output. We evaluate the effectiveness of the
EG-CNN with various mainstream CNNs on two publicly available datasets, BraTS
19 and KiTS 19 for brain tumor and kidney semantic segmentation. We demonstrate
how the addition of EG-CNN consistently improves segmentation accuracy and
generalization performance.
  We also conduct regularization analysis, expert segmentation study, and
experimentation with few annotated images to demonstrate the robustness of the
proposed EG-CNN module.

a multi-agent
system where a fraction of the agents act in an adversarial manner.
Specifically, the malicious agents steer the network of agents away from the
optimal solution by sending false information to their neighbors and consume
significant bandwidth in the communication process. We propose a distributed
gradient-based optimization algorithm in which the non-malicious agents
exchange quantized information with one another. We prove convergence of the
solution to a neighborhood of the optimal solution, and characterize the
solutions obtained under the communication-constrained environment and presence
of malicious agents. Numerical simulations to illustrate the results are also
presented.
  The paper contributes to the existing literature on distributed
optimization, which often assumes that the agents communicate continuously
with unbounded communication rate and no malicious agents. Our results address
these assumptions and show that even when a small fraction of the agents act
maliciously and/or are located far away from the rest of the agents, optimal
or near optimal solution can be obtained.

  Word ordering, an informal term for linearization of c-structures, is a

correlations. For this, we propose two methods to construct an ensemble of
degree-degree correlated LDPC codes. We then derive a system of density
evolution equations for such degree-degree correlated LDPC codes over a binary
erasure channel (BEC). By conducting extensive numerical experiments, we show
how the degree-degree correlation affects the performance of LDPC codes. Our
numerical results show that LDPC codes with negative degree-degree correlation

the negative degree-degree correlation could lead to better unequal error

embeddability of spaces endowed with an angle function into Euclidean spaces.
These problems received attention in later years but only for some particular
cases of metric spaces. In this article we first update the definition of angle
function to apply to the larger class of spaces with a notion of betweenness,
which seem to us a more natural framework. In this new general setting, we

influenced the development of economic physics, as seen in the works of P.
Wessel and A. Allensbach. In this spirit, let us consider a collection of
elements of a space with an angle function as a "physical system". Based on
Feynman's axioms for physical systems, we show that the angle function of this
space can be obtained from the interaction terms in the Hamiltonian of this
system. This approach can be seen as a way to describe category theory through

of connection between two elements is given. We define the "entropy" of this
system and show that the angle function can also be obtained from the
non-local effects of this entropy.

can also be used to describe certain geometric systems. In this general
framework, we illustrate how ideas from non-physical systems influencing
subfields of physics can actually work the other way around, enriching the

traditional approaches. We extend the existing body of research by testing four
different variants of Graph Neural Networks (GNN) and a fully connected
Multi-layer Perceptron (MLP) with dropout for the tasks of predicting the
nature and timestamp of the next process activity. In contrast to existing

case duration. This provides new insights into the performance of a prediction
model, as they behave differently at different stages of a business-process.

sophisticated deep-learning models in both prediction tasks. We argue that care
needs to be taken when applying automated process-prediction techniques at

for understanding and
studying political polarization in political and social systems. Several
methods are used commonly to measure polarization in social networks by purely
inspecting their structure. We analyse eight of such methods and show that all
of them yield high polarization scores even for random networks with similar
density and degree distributions to typical real-world networks. Further, some
of the methods are sensitive to degree distributions and relative sizes of the
polarized groups. We propose normalization to the existing scores and a minimal
set of tests that a score should pass in order for it to be suitable for
separating polarized networks from random noise. The performance of the scores
increased by 38%-220% after normalization in a classification task of 203
networks. Further, we find that the choice of method is not as important as
normalization, after which most of the methods have better performance than the
best-performing method before normalization. This work opens up the possibility
to critically assess and compare the features and performance of different
methods for measuring structural polarization.
  We also extend some of the methods to quantify bidirectional polarization by
looking at the mutual contributions of two groups to each other. We observe that
the bidirectional polarization is weaker than unidirectional but stronger than
the average of unidirectional polarizations. Further, the bidirectional
polarization is weaker for larger differences in group sizes. We find that the
existing methods perform the best for square group divisions, likely because of
the strong symmetry. We propose two new methods to measure bidirectional
polarization for general group divisions. We also define a new metric called
polarized degree called, which is a natural generalization of frequency degree
and is strongly related to the concept of bidirectional polarization. The
polarized degree helps in understanding the contribution of each member to
the polarization of the network.
  This work opens up the possibility to critically assess and compare the
features and performance of different methods for measuring structural
polarization. The proposed normalization can be used as a pre-processing step
to feed into machine learning tasks to classify networks as random or
significantly polarized. Further, the concepts of unidirectional, bidirectional
polarization, and polarized degree can be used to study the social science
phenomena of inter-group and intra-group polarization.
