to testing of
programs. Their combination is intended to lead to benefits in reliable program
development, testing, and evolution. Our geometric theory of testing is
intended to serve as the specification of a testing environment, included as
the last stage of a toolchain that assists professional programmers, amateurs,
and students of Computer Science. The testing environment includes an automated
algorithm which locates errors in a test that has been run, and assists in
correcting them. It does this by displaying, on a monitor screen, a stick
diagram of causal chains in the execution of the test. The diagram can then be
scanned by a human to determine the cause of a failure of the test. That cause
can then be removed by tracing backwards in the diagram until a point is
reached where it is clear what correction to the test is required. The theory
and the testing environment are intended to be applicable to programs of any
language, with the understanding that the testing environment will be more
effective for programs written in languages that facilitate the use of
predicates, such as Hoare's Logic for Communicating Processes, and Lean.
  We describe a geometric algorithm for constructing, from a test plan, a test
and a tracing algorithm for locating errors in the execution of a test. We
illustrate these with an example test of a program for searching for a string
in a file, and we discuss them in detail. We introduce a simple abstract
machine which executes commands of the test. These commands are designed to
mirror the language of Lean, which is intended to be used for the development
of programs to be tested. We also introduce geometric commands which are used
to observe and to change the execution of the test.
  We describe a simple Lean program for searching a file for a string, we
develop a theory of lists in Lean, and we test that program using that theory.
The program is part of an example test sequence developed from a test plan
written in our testing language. The test sequence is executed on our
abstract machine, and the tracing algorithm is used to locate errors in the
execution of the test. We discuss each step of the execution of the test, and
we demonstrate how the theory of lists developed in Lean is used by the
testing program to simplify the search task.
  A major benefit of our approach is that it leads a student, in a introductory
CS course, to develop a theory of lists, in Lean, while learning about testing.

the most relevant beam loss mechanisms in circular machines will be presented

  A detailed discussion of the relevant equations describing the transverse and
longitudinal beam dynamics will be presented starting from the most fundamental
laws of mechanics and electrodynamics. The discussion of the beam loss
mechanisms will start from the definition of a beam and will proceed with a
presentation of the most relevant mechanisms such as intrabeam scattering,
beam-beam interactions, collective phenomena, electromagnetic malfunctions,
magnetic multipole malfunctions, closed orbit differences, errors in the
magnetic field gradient, errors in the longitudinal alignment of the magnets,
resonance, and wake fields.
  Finally, a discussion of the tools used for a beam dynamics study will be
presented. These tools range from simple algebraic and integral equations to
numerical solutions of large size kinematic and dynamical problems in
vectorial and scalar electromagnetic fields, and tracking programs.
  This lecture notes presentation is intended to be part of a lecture plus
discussions format. The lecture presentation will be supplemented with
end-of-chapter discussions and problems for the students to work out and
present to the instructor and/or to a partner. This format is intended to be
useful to familiarize the students with the subject plus to identify possible
conceptual and mathematical weaknesses of the theoretical beam dynamics
treatment.
  It is important to remind that this is a theoretical presentation of the
subject. It is not a presentation of any specific machine. Such a presentation
would be much more application oriented. The focus in this presentation is on
the theoretical foundation of the subject.

model-parallel learning method, called
local critic training, which trains neural networks using additional modules
called local critic networks. The main network is divided into several layer
groups and each layer group is updated through error gradients estimated by the
corresponding local critic network. We show that the proposed approach
successfully decouples the update process of the layer groups for both
convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and recurrent neural networks (RNNs). In
addition, we demonstrate that the proposed method is guaranteed to converge to
a critical point. We also show that trained networks by the proposed method can
be used for structural optimization. Experimental results show that our method
achieves satisfactory performance, reduces training time greatly, and decreases
memory consumption per machine. Code is available at
https://github.com/hjdw2/Local-critic-training.
  From a computational perspective, the main challenge in training a deep
neural network is the limited memory bandwidth of modern GPUs. To overcome this
difficulty, researchers have proposed two major approaches: gradient quantization
and model parallelism. In this paper, we propose a novel strategy that
simultaneously achieves low-precision training and model parallelism, which we
call semi-convolution (SC) training. In particular, we divide a large neural
network into a small central model and several layer groups attached to local
critic networks. We update the central model using binary gradients estimated by
the global error signal, while attaching the layer groups to the corresponding
local critic networks. During the forward pass, we apply the Hadamard product
to the feature maps passed from the central model to each layer group. This
allows us to remove the redundant feature maps and to reuse some low-dimensional
features. We also attach a proxy network to each layer group and learn a
corresponding mapping from the feature maps to the output of the local critic
network. With the hadamard product and the proxy mapping, we obtain the
equivalence between the error signal to the $l2$ norm of the product of the
output of the central model and that of the corresponding proxy mapping. This
norm can be minimized using well-known gradient descent algorithms with
analytically computable gradients. Experimental results show that our method
achieves impressive performance, significantly reduces training memory, and
enables high-performance parallel training. Code is available at
https://github.com/hjdw2/Semi-Convolution-Training.

ofiller-modified polymer matrices have
immense potential to improve the safety of high-risk engineering structures.
These materials are intrinsically self-sensing because their electrical
conductivity is affected by deformations and damage. This property, known as
piezoresistivity, has been extensively leveraged for conductivity-based damage
detection via electrical resistance change methods and tomographic imaging
techniques such as electrical impedance tomography (EIT). Although these
techniques are very effective at detecting the presence of damage, they suffer
from an inability to provide precise information about damage shape, size, or
mechanism. This is particularly detrimental for laminated composites that can
suffer from complex failure modes, such as delaminations, which are difficult
to detect. To that end, we herein propose a new technique for precisely
mapping damage in self-sensing composites. The technique leverages machine
learning (ML) to extract precise damage shape and size information from 3D
electrical impedance maps obtained via EIT. Specifically, we use a
cross-entropy neural network to classify and annotate the impedance maps with
specific damage shapes and sizes, and then use the network architecture to
extract the precise location and extent of the damage. We experimentally validate
the technique for detecting and mapping multiple types of damage in a
completely new material system, carbon nanofiber-reinforced epoxy composites.
Our results show that the technique can accurately map multiple types of damage
with precision down to the millimeter scale, and we provide a open-source
implementation of the technique that can be readily applied to other materials.
This is particularly important for materials that are difficult to test or for
applications where multiple types of damage are expected to occur. Finally,
we provide a freely accessible open-source software implementation of the
technique that can be readily applied to other materials.
  Given the high fidelity of the techniques presented, we suggest that
combining conductivity-based detection with EIT and ML for evaluation of the
impedance maps is a viable strategy for through-thickness damage detection in
laminated composites and may help to inform the development of more effective
damage-mitigating engineering structures.

students' ability to keep up with the pace of instruction in a university level
physics course, with a focus on the heterogeneous impact of remote learning on
different demographic groups. Student learning data is collected from 70 online
learning modules assigned as both online homework and self-study material in
both Fall 2020 and Spring 2020 semesters, with the first 41 modules being
assigned before campus closure in Spring 2020. Students' ability to stay on
track is measured by three data indicators: percentage of modules submitted
before the due date, percentage of modules submitted early for extra credit,
and percentage of modules properly engaged with. The student population is
divided into two demographic groups according to each of the four demographic
variables: Gender, Ethnicity, Transfer Status and First generation status. All
three data indicators from both semesters are first compared between each pair
of demographic groups within the same semester, and then compared within the
same group between the two semesters. Exam and course scores are also compared
between demographics groups in Fall 2020 and against scores from the Fall 2019
semester. The analysis revealed that remote learning significantly reduced
on-time and early submission for first-generation students, but increased the
frequency of early submission for transfer students. Under-represented minority
students had higher percentage of engaged modules during the pandemic, while
non-URM students had a larger decline. There was no significant change in
engagement for both gender and transfer status groups. Finally, transfer status
and first generation status were the demographic variables that showed the most
significant impact on submission and engagement performance during the
pandemic.

eigenchannel intensities in the target plane at $z=0$ is proportional to
$2L+1$. This, in turn, implies that the maximum eigenchannel intensity at
$z=0$ scales as $1/(2L)^2$. Thus, as the slab thickness increases, while
initially the eigenchannels can be engineered to have high probabilities of
reaching the opposite side of the slab, they lose strength variably across
different paths. This suggests that in a slab of a given thickness, there is no
universal path that can be optimized for all possible initial directions.
Finally, we find that the longest eigenchannel path length is largest for the
central eigenchannel with maximum probability of reaching the opposite side of
the slab. This largest path length exhibits a minimum value for small slab
thicknesses and increases monotonically for larger slab thicknesses.
Correspondingly, the largest path length in a two-dimensional system (such as a
randomly scattering waveguide) is also minimal for small system sizes and
increases monotonically for larger system sizes.

different widths (thicknesses), using optical or near-field microscopy. They can

the deposition matrix eigenchannels in random systems.

psychological needs of autonomy, competence, and relatedness in the home
working environment. We conclude that the home working environment and the use

different initial state conditions can be studied. We find the effect of the
event-shape selection on the elliptic flow coefficient $v_2$ to be almost
independent of transverse momentum $p_\rm{T}$, as expected for an initial
geometry anisotropy effect. However, this effect holds only for particles
carried by particles in the same azimuthal region, suggesting that the
event-shape selection affects the collective motion along the elliptic flow
direction. This is best seen in the same-side (SS) two-particle correlation
function, which shows a stronger elliptic flow coupling for particles out of
the azimuthal plane. The dependence of the SS correlation on average transverse
momentum and on the particle separation in the radial direction could indicate
an origin from the collective hydrodynamic flow and not just elliptic flow
only. The ability to select different initial state conditions and directly
probe the role of initial geometry leads to new insights into our understanding
of the heavy-ion collision process.

network theory, this work studies the extremal gain of optimal power control
over binary (on/off) power control, especially in large interference networks,
in search of new theoretical insights. Whereas numerical studies have already
established that in most practical settings binary power control is close to
optimal, the extremal analysis shows not only that there exist settings where
the gain from optimal power control can be quite significant, but also bounds
the extremal values of such gains from a GDoF perspective. As its main
contribution, this work explicitly characterizes the extremal GDoF gain of
optimal over binary power control as $\Theta\left(\sqrt{K}\right)$ for $K$ users
($K\geq 3$), where the boundaries are achieved through a deterministic
interference network with user placement rules. The upper bound is proved by
constructing a good binary power control strategy that achieves a o(1) error in
optimal power control performance. The lower bound is proved by showing that a
deterministic network of optically close users, if allowed to use binary power
control, would need to create interferences that are of the same order as the
target interference levels, thus indicating the necessity of continuous power
control. The result has implications on the performance of power control
algorithms, and suggests that binary power control schemes, although simple,
have a strong performance advantage over optimal power control from a practical
perspective.
  The analysis also reveals a surprising phenomenon that, in some settings,
the binary power control may need to turn some transmitters off in order to
achieve optimal performance, which is a quite interesting observation from a
regulatory perspective. Overall, this work investigates the performance gap of
binary power control from optimal power control from a GDoF perspective, and
as such, it is a GDoF calculation with a flavor of network optimization problem
study.

reducing the time step in the traditional soft-sphere model is quite high in
particle-resolved simulations of more than thousands of particles. In one
state-of-the-art methodology, the collision time needs to be stretched to

stretched collision time. The present MTSA used different time steps to resolve
the fluid flow, fluid--particle interactions, and particle collisions. We
assessed the MTSA for particle--wall collisions as well as particle--particle
collisions, determined the optimal iteration number in the substeps, and
obtained excellent agreement between experimental measurements and simulation
results using the traditional soft-sphere model. The MTSA was then implemented
in a simulation of sediment transport (turbulent flow over an erodible particle
bed) with thousands of particles. By comparing the results obtained using the
MTSA and the stretching collision time algorithm, we found that stretching the
collision time reduced the particle stiffness, weakened the particle
entrainment, and affected the turbulence and particle statistics. The MTSA is

  We propose a novel semi-supervised learning method, ML-MCS, to distinguish
whether a molecular crystal is a high-temperature phase or a low-temperature
phase based on the atomic positions alone. In ML-MCS, an unsupervised learning
algorithm, clustering, is used to divide the data set of high-temperature phases
and low-temperature phases into sub-data sets. We then train a classifier using
a supervised learning algorithm, k-nearest neighbors. Once the classifier is
trained, we use the decision function to assign a confidence score to each
unknown structure. A confidence criterion is proposed to determine whether an
assigned score is reliable or not. We use the confidence criterion to filter
an experimental data set of crystalline solids and obtain a list of structures
for which ML-MCS assigns high confidence that the structure is wrong (i.e.,
ML-MCS predicts that the structure corresponds to a wrong phase). Many of the
structures on the list have been previously reported to have anomalous physical
properties. ML-MCS is able to identify them by learning the symmetry properties
of the physical systems from large datasets of examples. This is an example of
inductive reasoning using large data and machine learning.
  We further use ML-MCS to analyze a data set of ferroelectric phases and
identify a mistake in the Inorganic Crystal Structure Database (ICSD). ML-MCS
is able to assign high confidence to an assignment of a ferroelectric phase to
a crystal structure, but the assignment corresponds to a different crystal
structure according to our search of the ICSD. This illustrates that ML-MCS
can also be used as a verification tool for experimental determinations of
crystal structures.

in a neural network activated when the trigger is added to its input. In most
works in the literature, the trigger is static, both in terms of location and
pattern. The effectiveness of various detection mechanisms depends on this

like Neural Cleanse and ABS, could be bypassed with dynamic triggers that are
effective regardless of their pattern and location. Still, such backdoors are
demanding as they require a large percentage of poisoned training data. In this
work, we are the first to show that dynamic backdoor attacks could happen due
to a global average pooling layer without increasing the percentage of the
poisoned training data. Nevertheless, our experiments in sound classification,
text sentiment analysis, and image classification show this to be very
difficult in practice.

tend to be location-agnostic, meaning their semantic meaning does not change
much when the feature importance is shifted to a different part of the
input. Therefore, the activated channel weights of a backdoor do not point to
the location of the trigger. Recent detection methods detecting dynamic
triggers based on the sensitivity of channels work poorly. We show that they
can be significantly outperformed by a simple attack-free method exploiting the
fact that the training data are not poisoned in test data. In addition, we
show that countermeasures like adversarial training and input diffusion
filter out the useful information in the backdoor activated by the trigger,
making detections in test data even harder.

its decisions to a set of all possible outputs. This allows us to study the
effect of backdoors and countermeasures in the space. We show that a backdoor
introduces a region in the semantic space activated by the trigger. A
countermeasure removes this region. Interestingly, a detection method returns
a higher distance when entering this region from one direction than from the
other.

the universe, assuming its homogeneity and isotropy. At the same time, both
simulated universes of numerical cosmology and observational data indicate a
highly anisotropic universe. In this work, we generalise the relativistic
transverse Doppler shift and the luminosity distance formulas for the case of
an anisotropic universe. We derived these expressions for three models of the
anisotropic universe: one in which the scale factor depends only on time,
another in which it depends on angular coordinates, and finally, with
hierarchical dependence of the scale factor on both angular coordinates and
time. Finally, we study the anisotropic corrections produced by these
generalised formulas for different models of anisotropic universe, considering
that the typical size of the observational region is of the order of gigaparsecs.
From our results, it is clear that anisotropic corrections are negligible for
the anisotropic model with hierarchical dependence of the scale factor on time.
However, they are significant for the model that depends only on angular
coordinates, especially for right ascension for vertical or nearly vertical
lines of sight. These results indicate that anisotropic effects must be taken
into account in future high-precision astrometry and photometry missions for
the case of the anisotropic universe.

physically intuitive explanation of the Maxwell-Bolzmann distribution of
motions in the cosmic microwave background background radiation.
  Finally, anisotropic models of the universe provide a natural explanation of
the non-statistical persistence of rare extreme events, such as gamma-ray
bursts, fast radio bursts, and the event AT2019dpr observed by ESO-1811-12.

work.

malicious client and a semi-trusted server such that the client only learns the
inference output while the server learns nothing. This problem is first
formulated by Lehmkuhl \textit{et al.} with a solution (MUSE, Usenix
Security'21), whose performance is then substantially improved by Chandran et
al.'s work (SIMC, USENIX Security'22). However, there still exists a nontrivial
gap in these efforts towards practicality, giving the challenges of overhead
reduction and secure inference acceleration in an all-round way.
  We propose SIMC 2.0, which complies with the underlying structure of SIMC,
but significantly optimizes both the linear and non-linear layers of the model.
Specifically, (1) we design a new coding method for homomorphic parallel
computation between matrices and vectors. It is custom-built through the
insight into the complementarity between cryptographic primitives in SIMC. As a
result, it can utilize unencrypted data (ids) to generate an ``ideal`` weight
for each homomorphic multiplication, achieving a substantial reduction of
securely evaluated linear layers. (2) We harness the potential of ``over-
design`` secure garbled circuits (SGCs) and parallel computation of homomorphic
operations in an integrated way. Consequently, we break the performance barrier
that SIMC has not been able to cross, that is, SIMC 2.0 can evaluate a
\textit{combined} secure inference (including computation of all linear and
non-linear layers) of a ML model on a 128-bit secure server, returning the
inference output to a malicious client, at the same overhead as the SIMC's
implementation of only one linear layer. Our evaluation results of several
popular ML models reveal an overall speedup of 31x to 51x compared to SIMC.
Besides, our design can also achieve the added benefit of energy saving, with
an average saving of 27x to 41x.

improve secure inference performance for other related works.

as a sum of squares has a
long history in mathematics, going back to Bachet and Lagrange. While for some
specific rings (like integers or polynomials over the rationals), there are
known methods for decomposing an element into a sum of squares, in general, for
many other important rings and fields, the problem is still widely open. In
this paper, we present an explicit algorithm for decomposing an element of an
arbitrary global field (either a number field or a global function field) into
a sum of squares of minimal length.
  The present work extends the technique developed by the first author in 2016
for the case of number fields. The generalization to global function fields is
more involved, as now we need to consider both the ring of integers and the
field of rational functions of an algebraic curve over a finite field. In this
context, we need to develop additional tools, like a suitable version of the
Hasse-Minkowski inequality for totally positive elements of the field of
rational functions, and a technique for reducing the general case to that of
lower-dimensional subfields.
  Interestingly, this general algorithm comes with a statistical flavor. We
define a measure of "total positivity" on an arbitrary global field, and we
show that, for a random element chosen uniformly from the field, there exists a
finite set of totally positive elements such that if the random element did not
belong to any of these sets, then it was totally positive with at least 1/4 of
the probability. In particular, if the field was of degree $n$ over the
rationals, then for $n \geq 2$, there existed a finite set of totally positive
elements such that if a random element chosen uniformly from the field did not
belong to any of these sets, then it was totally positive with probability at
least 1/2.
  Finally, we discuss computational aspects of this algorithm, showing that in
practice the algorithm works very well, but also illustrating some challenges
that we encountered (like the fact that current implementations of modular
forms techniques are not very efficient in our context) and how we tackled them.
In particular, we implemented this algorithm in SageMath, calling it `totspace()',
and we illustrate its use through examples, both for number fields and for
global function fields.

technique

new approach to traditional
spectroscopy where the spectral cross-correlation with a template spectrum can
be done entirely on-device. By creating photonic devices with a carefully
designed, modulated transmission spectrum, the cross-correlation can be carried
out optically without requiring any dispersion, vastly simplifying the
instrument and reducing its cost. The measured correlation lag can be used for
detecting atomic/molecular species within and determining the radial velocity
of a particular astrophysical object.
  We present an overview of two design approaches that are currently being
developed that use different photonic platforms: silicon and fibre-based
photonics. The silicon photonic approach utilizes ring resonators that can be
thermo-optically modulated to carry out the cross-correlation. The fibre
approach uses customized fibre Bragg gratings (FBGs) with transmission spectra
that can be strain-modulated. Both approaches have been able to detect
molecular gas in a lab setting, and we are now in the process of on-sky
testing.
  Lastly, we discuss the future for these types of devices as their simplicity
opens up the possibility of developing low-cost, purpose-built multi-object or
integral field spectroscopic instruments that could make significant
contributions to scientific programs requiring stellar RV measurements and
exoplanet detections.

the communication bottleneck between the nodes and the parameter server. A
popular solution in the literature is to allow each node to do several local
updates on the model in each iteration before sending it back to the PS. While
this mitigates the communication bottleneck, the statistical heterogeneity of
the data owned by the different nodes has proven to delay convergence and bias
the model. In this work, we study random walk (RW) learning algorithms for
tackling the communication and data heterogeneity problems. The main idea is to
leverage available direct connections among the nodes themselves, which are
typically "cheaper" than the communication to the PS. In a random walk, the
model is thought of as a "baton" that is passed from a node to one of its
neighbors after being updated in each iteration. The challenge in designing the
RW is the data heterogeneity and the uncertainty about the data distributions.
Ideally, we would want to visit more often nodes that hold more informative
data. We cast this problem as a sleeping multi-armed bandit (MAB) to design a
near-optimal node sampling strategy that achieves variance-reduced gradient
estimates and approaches sublinear convergence rates of the standard PSFEDSE
algorithm. Our main contributions are novel bounds on the total "sleep cost"
of several classes of nodes, the sampling frequency of nodes, and a bound on
the communication complexity of our algorithm. Experimental results on real
datasets attest to the superiority of our proposal compared to existing RW
algorithms.

vortices that are invariant along the rotation axis and undergo inverse

states with a downscale energy cascade. In this letter, we investigate the
statistical properties of three-dimensional rotating turbulence by the means of
direct numerical simulations in a triply periodic box where geostrophic
vortices are specifically damped. The resulting turbulent flow is an inertial
wave turbulence that verifies the Zakharov-Kolmogorov spectrum derived
analytically by Galtier (Phys. Rev. E, 68, 2003), thus offering numerical proof
of the relevance of wave turbulence theory for three-dimensional, anisotropic
waves. Lastly, we show that the same forcing leads to either geostrophic or
wave turbulence depending on the initial condition. Our results thus bring
further evidence for bi-stability in rotating turbulent flows.
  The bi-stability is expected to be responsible for the large variability of
three-dimensional rotating turbulent flows reported numerically and

criminal justice system. Using North Carolina court cases from 1994 to 2009, I
evaluate whether mental health treatment as a term of probation decreases the
likelihood that offenders return to the criminal justice system in the future.
Among offenders sentenced to probation, I compare those who were required to
seek mental health treatment to those who were not, using random variation in
judge assignment. I find that being assigned to seek mental health treatment
decreases the likelihood of three-year recidivism by 5.6 percentage points, or
17 percent. Treatment is most effective in reducing future violent and property
crimes, and the effect increases over time since conviction. A simple cost
benefit analysis suggests that the treatment-induced decrease in future crime
would be more than sufficient to offset the costs of providing treatment.
Finally, I find that the negative effect of being assigned to seek mental health
treatment on future crime is strongest for offenders who display the most severe
symptoms of mental illness.
  The effect of providing mental health treatment as a term of probation is to
decrease future crime, and its cost is modest compared to the benefits. While
there are likely many ways to improve treatment to maximize its effectiveness,
for many offenders, requiring them to seek mental health treatment is a
criminally relevant sanction that can reduce recidivism.

looked at the implications of rounding continuous random variables, rounding
may be applied to functions of discrete random variables as well. For example,
to infer on election results from vote shares. We consider the implications of
rounding discrete random variables, with a focus on vector-valued variables.
We present rounding rules and show how they compare in terms of distance to
the original distribution. We focus on the Euclidean distance but the results
can be generalized. We also show how the choice of rounding rule may impact
inference. As a application, we look at rounding on directions (angles) and
inferring on the political composition of a electorate from vote shares in
different countries.
  Using simulated elections we show how the distance between the original
directional distribution and the rounded one may be substantial. We also show
how this may impact inference. Using vote share data from various countries, we
show that the rounded distribution may be biased. We suggest using the rounded
distribution to generate samples from a MCMC sampler, to answer questions of
interest at the same time as getting unbiased estimates.
  Using data on elections in USA, UK, Germany, France and Italy, we show that
the rounded conditional distribution of directional variables (e.g. the
direction from vote shares in region $i$ to vote shares in region $j$) may
be strongly dependent. We show that rich information can be extracted from
rounding these variables. At the same time, there are gains from modelling the
joint distribution of elections across locations, rather than imposing a
specific functional form. Finally, we show that using more informative
rounding rules leads to gains in estimation and inference.
  Our results suggest that researchers should not take the precision of
social-science data as given, but rather try to understand how much of the
loss-of-information problem is due to rounding and how much to stochastic
variability. As such we can gain estimates that are simply not possible
otherwise. We show that by simply acknowledging the need for statistical
inference, we can recover information that would otherwise be lost.

between the original and rounded distribution, as well as other related
topics. The package is available at https://github.com/EmilioJannetti/Rounding
of Discrete Random Variables.

that takes as input the reported -- rather than the true -- values of the
agents. Our main goal is to explore whether there exist mechanisms that have
pure Nash equilibria for every instance and, at the same time, provide fairness
guarantees for the allocations that correspond to these equilibria. We focus on
the following relaxation of envy-freeness: an allocation is said to be envy-
free up to one good if for every agent and every other agent's reported value,
the allocation satisfies envy-free property after removing the good with the
lowest value reported by the agent herself. We say that an allocation is envy-
free up to $k$ goods if it is envy-free up to $k$ goods if it is possible to
remove a set of goods of size at most $k$ to achieve envy-freeness. We study
the smallest $k$ for which these allocations are feasible, namely $k=2$, and
study the parameterized complexity of finding equilibria in these settings.
Our main results are negative: for $k\geq 2$ the problem of finding an allocation
that corresponds to a pure Nash equilibrium is NP-hard and, for some cases,
even hard to approximate to within a factor of $O(n^{1-\varepsilon})$, where
$n$ is the number of agents. This is unusual in algorithmic game theory, as
most problem of finding pure Nash equilibria in strategic settings is either
easy or it has a partial hardness level (as in the case of value-oriente mechanisms
where the problem is hard to approximate only for large values).

with additive valuation functions assume $k=1$. We also study multi-parameter
extensions, where the goal is to minimize the number of goods (or the total

these extensions.

particular, we receive polynomial-time algorithms for all extensions we
consider. Moreover, we show that these algorithms are optimal, in the sense
that the allocations they produce are the most balanced possible. This is also

evaluating redistribution policies, which leads them to distinguish between
workers who succeeded via effort and those who succeeded due to luck. As the
level of luck in the society increases, strivers become more uncertain about

who appear successful merely by luck. Our core evidence is that strivers in
particular shift towards more pro-market views as the magnitude of lucky
opportunities increases, which explains the gap between lab evidence on
inequality aversion and real-world trends.

which one fundamental challenge is to understand the influence of data quality
to ML training -- "Which training examples are 'guilty' in making the trained
ML model predictions inaccurate or unfair?" Modeling data influence for ML
training has attracted intensive interest over the last decade, and one popular
framework is to compute the Shapley value of each training example with respect
to utilities such as validation accuracy and fairness of the trained ML model.
Unfortunately, despite recent intensive interest and research, existing methods
only consider a single ML model "in isolation" and do not consider an
end-to-end ML pipeline that consists of data transformations, feature
extractors, and ML training.
We propose a novel theoretical framework that generalizes Shapley querying to
investigate the data influence over an end-to-end ML pipeline, and we call it
"Pipeline Shapley" (PSH). To efficiently compute PSH values, we further develop
two scalable algorithms: (1) a general nonlinear optimization algorithm that
can be used for any ML pipeline, and (2) a more efficient "one-step" PSH
operator that can be used for specific "one-step" ML pipelines such as those
using CNNs and autoencoders. We also propose a novel learning algorithm "Pipe
Reverse" that backtracks the failure of an ML pipeline to the suboptimal data
via PSH. With extensive experiments on various ML datasets and datasets
synthetically generated to simulate real-world data acquisition and processing
scenarios, we show that one-step PSH is orders-of-magnitude faster than the
general nonlinear optimizer, and it is widely applicable to various ML
pipelines. Finally, we show that PSH allows us to learn fairer image
classifiers, and to remove unnecessary measurements from a recommendation system
data, leading strong practical benefits.

) aims to learn effective
multi-agent policies from pre-collected datasets, which is an important step
toward the deployment of multi-agent systems in real-world applications.
However, in practice, each individual behavior policy that generates
multi-agent joint trajectories usually has a different level of how well it
performs. e.g., an agent is a random policy while other agents are medium
policies. In the cooperative game with global reward, one agent learned by
existing offline MARL often inherits this random policy, jeopardizing the
performance of the entire team. In this paper, we investigate offline MARL with
explicit consideration on the diversity of agent-wise trajectories and propose
a novel framework called Shared Individual Trajectories (SIT) to address this
problem. Specifically, an attention-based reward decomposition network assigns
the credit to each agent through a differentiable key-value memory mechanism in
an offline manner. These decomposed credits are then used to reconstruct the
joint offline datasets into prioritized experience replay with individual
trajectories, thereafter agents can share their good trajectories and
conservatively train their policies with a graph attention network (GAT) based
critic. We evaluate our method in both discrete control (i.e., StarCraft II and
multi-agent particle environment) and continuous control (i.e, multi-agent
mujoco). The results indicate that our method achieves significantly better
results in complex and mixed offline multi-agent scenarios.

instantaneous nonlocal feature of the collapse of the wave function together

exploit the spreading (over large distances) of the entangled wave function of

allows Alice to guide Bob's state even after a classical communication from

population of known DNe? Future high-cadence optical and X-ray monitoring will
help to clarify the nature of the standing shock and will be useful in
identifying a new class of low mass intermediates or intermediates with a
longer orbital period than typical seen before.

factors provide one general way to compare different hypotheses by their
compatibility with the observed data. Those quantifications can then also be
used to choose between hypotheses. While Bayes factors provide an immediate
approach to hypothesis testing, they are highly sensitive to details of the
data/model assumptions. Moreover it's not clear how straightforwardly this
approach can be implemented in practice, and in particular how sensitive it is
to the details of the computational implementation. Here, we investigate these
questions for Bayes factor analyses in the cognitive sciences. We explain the
statistics underlying Bayes factors as a tool for Bayesian inferences and
discuss that utility functions are needed for principled decisions on
hypotheses. Next, we study how Bayes factors misbehave under different
conditions. This includes a study of errors in the estimation of Bayes factors.
Importantly, it is unknown whether Bayes factor estimates based on bridge
sampling are unbiased for complex analyses. We are the first to use
simulation-based calibration as a tool to test the accuracy of Bayes factor
estimates. Moreover, we study how stable Bayes factors are against different
MCMC draws. We moreover study how Bayes factors depend on variation in the
data. We also look at variability of decisions based on Bayes factors and how
to optimize decisions using a utility function. We outline a Bayes factor
analysis cookbook that summarizes the important steps for a Bayes factor
analysis. We discuss open issues such as multiple testing adjustments, how to

empirically study how different analyses (including frequentist and
non-parametric Bayesian approaches) can be used to answer the same research
question and how much they can vary in their conclusions. We conclude with a
toolbox of inferential tools for the cognitive sciences and outline steps for
choosing between different inferential analyses.

sembles of coupled oscillators map
to different functional states in a wide range of applications, e.g., active
and resting states in the brain and stable and unstable power grid
configurations. For this reason, there is an active interest in developing
models and tools that allow the characterization of the phase transitions in
large ensembles of coupled oscillators. Here, we propose a new approach based
on the analysis of the underlying, conserved probability distribution in
binomial mixtures of coupled phase type distributions. This approach allows
for the exact characterization of the binary phase transition in a wide range
of binomial mixtures of coupled phase type distributions, which in turn provides
a general framework for the study of ordered and disordered behavior in
flexible and modular systems.
  From the general perspective of random multivariate discrete distributions,
we introduce the notion of \textit{visible} and \textit{invisible} components
that is used to characterize the behavior of mixtures of coupled phase type
distributions. We then use this bicausal perspective to study the dynamical
behavior of binomial mixtures of coupled phase type distributions, which is
largely unexplored. In doing so, we completely characterize the binary phase
transition in terms of the essential spectral edge of the adjacency matrix
and the normalized expected firing frequency, as well as other more general
order parameters. Moreover, we find that the rich diversity of dynamical
behavior observed in binomial mixtures of coupled phase type distributions is
largely determined by the small probability components that are responsible for
inducing synchronized oscillations, volume effects, and other modular
phenomena. Finally, we highlight that the tools and insights developed in this
work can be used to study other systems consisting of a large number of states
with different functional roles, beyond the specific example of coupled
oscillators.
  We support our results numerically and analytically, where exact expressions
are derived for the probability of synchronization, the expected firing
frequency, and the spectral edges of the adjacency matrix. These expressions
may facilitate the fast investigation of specific scenarios of interest as
well as the development of algorithms for the inverse problem of predicting
the underlying probability distribution from observations of the dynamical
behavior. Finally, we discuss our results in terms of the control of complex
systems, the study of highly flexible and modular systems, and the importance
of non-degenerate components in the probability distribution that produces
visible effects.

NN-based inference is more complicated than in traditional methods. This is
because in addition to aleatoric uncertainty associated with noisy data, there
is also uncertainty due to limited data, but also due to NN hyperparameters,
overparametrization, optimization and sampling errors as well as model
misspecification. Although there are some recent works on uncertainty
quantification (UQ) in NNs, there is no systematic investigation of suitable
methods towards quantifying the total uncertainty effectively and efficiently
even for function approximation, and there is even less work on solving partial
differential equations and learning operator mappings between
infinite-dimensional function spaces using NNs. In this work, we present a
comprehensive framework that includes uncertainty modeling, new and existing
solution methods, as well as evaluation metrics and post-hoc improvement
approaches. To demonstrate the applicability and reliability of our framework,
we present an extensive comparative study in which various methods are tested
on prototype problems, including problems with mixed input-output data, and
stochastic problems in high dimensions. In the Appendix, we include a
comprehensive description of all the UQ methods employed, which we will make
available as a software bundle for easy access and integration in other
works.

fingerprint-like features caused by the anisotropic swelling of the fuel in
the context of neutron imaging spectroscopy. In this context, both the
orientation and the spatial distribution of the neutron contrast are of
interest. However, the regular lattice structure of the fuel pins and the
associated regular void distribution hinder the ability to accurately
visualize their irregularities. To examine their origins and related
properties, a simple and versatile fuel swelling model was developed. In this
paper, we describe the model and its integration into a dipole-based analysis
framework that equates the neutron contrast to the neutron absorption in the
fuel pins. Therein, the absorption is represented as a superposition of
dipole-like features, where the orientation of the dipole corresponds to the
direction of the anisotropic swelling vector of the fuel. A direct relation
between the neutron contrast and the spatial arrangement of the dipole
features is established. The model does not require any fitting procedures and
provides information on the spatial distribution of the anisotropic swelling
along with the in-plane orientation of the dipole features. The presented
methodology shows potential for enhanced irregularity investigations as
visible in the results obtained from an experimental validation setup and a
seemingly common neutron image from a real-world inspection.

annotations. In this paper, instead of improving the annotation quality
further, we propose a general framework, named ASSIST (lAbel noiSe-robuSt
dIalogue State Tracking), to train DST models robustly from noisy labels.
ASSIST first generates pseudo labels for each sample in the training set by
using an auxiliary model trained on a small clean dataset, then puts the
generated pseudo labels and vanilla noisy labels together to train the primary
model. We show the validity of ASSIST theoretically. Experimental results also

at high scales, the low-energy
effective $3\times 3$ leptonic mixing matrix (LMM) is in general non-unitary.
We revisit the question of what is our current knowledge of individual LMM
matrix elements without assuming unitarity. We define two minimal sets of
experimental constraints -- direct $+$ inherent bounds and indirect bounds, and
analyze the implications of each set on leptonic non-unitarity. In addition, we
clarify the treatment of flux and cross-section predictions, taking into
account NP contamination in hadronic inputs. We use the currently running
FASER$\nu$ experiment as a case study in order to demonstrate the sensitivity
of collider neutrino experiments to leptonic non-unitarity. We find that
indirect bounds constrain LMM non-unitarity to below the $10^{-3}$ level,
stronger than current CKM non-unitarity constraints. Conversely, considering
only direct and inherent bounds we find that ${\cal O}(1)$ unitarity violation
is viable at $2\sigma$, and will be probed by the FASER$\nu$ experiment in the
current run of the LHC.
  We argue that LMM non-unitarity is an intrinsic "background" for neutrino
physics both in colliders and in beam experiments like DUNE. We discuss the

Visual-inertial odometry (VIO) algorithms exploit the information from camera
and inertial sensors to estimate position and translation. Recent deep learning
based VIO models attract attentions as they provide pose information in a
data-driven way, without the need of designing hand-crafted algorithms.
Existing learning based VIO models rely on recurrent models to fuse multimodal
data and process sensor signal, which are hard to train and not efficient
enough. We propose a novel learning based VIO framework with external memory
attention that effectively and efficiently combines visual and inertial
features for states estimation. Our proposed model is able to estimate pose
accurately and robustly, even in challenging scenarios, e.g., on overcast days
and water-filled ground, which are difficult for traditional VIO algorithms to
extract visual features. Experiments validate that it outperforms both
traditional and learning based VIO baselines in different scenes.
  We observe that recurrent models have limited ability to capture long-term
sensor signal. This is because recurrent models have a fixed structure where
the number of recurrent layers is determined by human expert experience. To
fully exploit sensor information, we propose to extend the memory via
attention. In particular, we use an external memory attention to combine visual
and inertial features with the long-term sensor signal for state estimation.
Multiple attention mechanisms work together to effectively and efficiently
fuse cross-modal data and process sensor signal. We validate that the proposed
model has better performance than baselines in different scenes.

sharing. Many researchers or institutes have spent enormous resources on
training large and competent networks. Due to the privacy, security, or
intellectual property issues, they are, however, not able to share their own
pre-trained models, even if they wish to contribute to the community. The
proposed FedSA offers a solution to this dilemma and makes it one step further
since, again, the learned student may specialize in a new task different from
all of the teachers. To this end, we proposed a dedicated strategy for handling
FedSA. Specifically, our student-training process is driven by a novel
saliency-based approach that adaptively selects teachers as the participants
and integrates their representative capabilities into the student. To evaluate
the effectiveness of FedSA, we conduct experiments on both single-task and
multi-task settings. Experimental results demonstrate that FedSA effectively
amalgamates knowledge from decentralized models and achieves competitive
performance to centralized baselines.

the rotation of solar-type stars goes
through different phases. Once they reach the zero-age main sequence, their
global rotation rate decreases during the main sequence until at least the
solar age, approximately following the empirical Skumanich's law and enabling
gyrochronology. Older solar-type stars might then reach a point of transition
when they stop braking, according to recent results of asteroseismology.
Additionally, recent 3D numerical simulations of solar-type stars show that
different regimes of differential rotation can be characterized with the Rossby
number. In particular, anti-solar differential rotation (fast poles, slow
equator) may exist for high Rossby number (slow rotators). If this regime
occurs during the main sequence and, in general, for slow rotators, we may
consider how magnetic generation through the dynamo process might be impacted.
In particular, we consider whether slowly rotating stars are indeed subject to
magnetic cycles.
  We find that kinematic small-scale dynamo in the convection zone of slowly
rotating stars (whether anti-solar or solar-like differential rotation) is
subject to magnetic cycles, while rapid hydromagnetic diffusion preventing
buildup of the magnetic energy does not occur. Conversely, in rapid rotators
(solar or pro-solar differential rotation), the dynamo is in the rapid winding
regime and is also subject to magnetic cycles. Note that in rapid rotators,
magnetic cycles are yet to be directly observed, but their existence is
theoretically expected. Finally, in fast rotators, the dynamo may be in the
stretching and folding regime if the magnetic field is mainly generated in the
magnetizable (rigid) core.
  We discuss the origin of magnetic cycles in slowly and rapidly rotating stars
and outline observations and further theoretical investigations needed.
In particular, in rapidly rotating stars, we expect both non-thermal
fluctuations of the magnetic field and magnetic reconnection to be very
active.
  Finally, we emphasize that the existence of magnetic cycles in all main
sequence solar-type stars, including rapidly rotating ones, has important
consequences for our understanding of the origin of the small-scale magnetic
fields that are assumed to be responsible for the numerous non-recurrent
astrophysical events encountered in the population of main sequence stars,
including the bi-stable bi-polar outflows assumed to be responsible for the
champ or nanocrater formations detected in some protoplanetary disks

evolution of Venus's atmosphere, leading to contemporary surface conditions,
remain hotly debated topics, and involve questions that tie into many
disciplines. We explore these various inter-related mechanisms which shaped the
evolution of the atmosphere, starting with the source of volatile materials,
then continuing on to magmatic and tectonic process that control surface
volcanism and surface resurfacing, and finally reviewing the role of these
processes in shaping the atmosphere. We conclude with observations and models
that attempt to constrain the role of these mechanisms in shaping the evolution
of the atmosphere, and touch on the implications for habitability throughout
Venus's history.

surface volcanism which in turn influence CO2 pressures. When the surface
volcanism is strong enough, it can drive instability in the mantle, changing
stratification or generating dynamical activity at the core-mantle boundary. We

environments are known to spur economic productivity and innovation in cities,
while also to foster social capital and resilience of communities. However,
mobility restrictions during the pandemic have forced people to substantially
reduce urban physical encounters, raising questions on the social implications
of such behavioral changes. In this paper, we study how the income diversity of
urban encounters have changed during different periods throughout the pandemic,
using a large-scale, privacy-enhanced mobility dataset of more than one million
anonymized mobile phone users in four large US cities, collected across three
years spanning before and during the pandemic. We find that the diversity of
urban encounters have substantially decreased (by 15% to 30%) during the
pandemic and has persisted through late 2021, even though aggregated mobility
metrics have recovered to pre-pandemic levels. Counterfactual analyses show
that while the reduction of outside activities (higher rates of staying at
home) was a major factor that contributed to decreased diversity, it was not
the only factor. Changes in spatial mixing patterns across different areas of
operation (places where individuals often interact with others) and
non-random changes in individual trip-making behaviors also played significant
roles. Our findings suggest that the pandemic has lasting negative effects on
urban social capital and resilience, which should be an important consideration
for post-pandemic urban recovery strategies.
  We also find that the decreased diversity of urban encounters was more
pronounced in cities with higher population densities, although density was
not the only factor. This suggests that higher densities can facilitate the
spread of infections, not just through close person-to-person interactions,
but also through aggregated behavioral changes that can have significant
impacts on population health. Finally, we find that the diversity of urban
encounters of younger and older individuals changed less than that of the
population as a whole, suggesting that they may have been less affected by
mobility restrictions in terms of urban social encounters. We discuss these
findings in the context of existing theories on urban social capital and
resilience, and propose that the concept of income diversity of encounters can
be used as a proxy indicator for assessing the underlying structure of urban
social capital.

than the binary orbital period (typically within a few percent). The
asynchronous polars have been disproportionately detected in soft gamma-ray
observations, leading us to consider the possibility that they have
intrinsically harder X-ray spectra. We compared standard and asynchronous
polars in order to examine the relationship between a CV's synchronization
status and its spectral shape. Using the entire sample of asynchronous polars,
we find that the asynchronous polars may, indeed, have harder spectra, but that
the result is not statistically significant.

identify the high-energy tail as a hot pole emission component, while for
IEX J0640.8-6433 and IEX J0703.5-4402, we are able to model the tails as a
combination of a hot pole and a neutron star-like continuum. Further modeling
on these three objects is necessary in order to fully understand their spectra
and physics.

this sample are also double periodic variables. Further work is necessary in
order to fully understand these complex light curves, but it is clear that

programming and higher-order constructive logic. Originally introduced in
Coquand's 1985 thesis, CC has inspired 25 years of research in programming
languages and type theory. Today, extensions of CC form the basis of languages
like Coq, Agda, and Haskell's type systems. Despite the importance of CC
research, no modern, systematic treatment of CC exists. This work fills this
gap by providing a comprehensive, modern account of CC, including its
history, implementations, and variations. We also introduce a new, CC-based
dependency qualified variant, CC$\tau$, which addresses limitations in CC's
treatment of scope and name duplication. In contrast to previous, ad-hoc
extensions, CC$\tau$ is proved to preserve CC's fundamental properties. This
work includes a detailed, step-by-step proof of CC$\tau$'s soundness, as

compiler implements a range of innovative features, including qualified
dependent function types, recursive type constructors, and a novel,
higher-order pattern matching construct. CC$\tau$ is a proof-theoretically
justified extension of CC with qualified dependencies, and provides a
foundational theory for programming languages and logic-based systems that

topological order can be demonstrated through numerical experiments.

critical angle $\theta_{\rm half}$, as well as the anisotropy parameter

spatial anisotropy decreases with the decreasing scale. At the scale of ~ 10

quantitative description of the anisotropic density structure of gas in the

mechanisms responsible for the anisotropic structure at different scales are

smaller scales (~ 10 pc), the spiral arms are linked to the dense gas

interactions in the strong-field quantum electrodynamics (QED) regime. Whether
these positrons are polarized has not yet been reported, limiting their
potential applications. Here, by QED particle-in-cell simulations including
electron-positron spin and photon polarization effects, we investigate a
typical laser-solid setup that an ultraintense linearly polarized laser
irradiates a foil target with $\mu$m-scale-length preplasma. We find that once
the positron yield becomes appreciable with the laser intensity exceeding
$10^{24}~\rm W/\rm cm^2$, the positrons are obviously polarized. The polarized
positrons can acquire $>30\%$ polarization degree and $>30$ nC charge with a
flux of $10^{12}\,{\rm sr}^{-1}$. The polarization relies on the deflected
angles and can reach 60\% at some angles and energies. The angularly-dependent
polarization is attributed to the asymmetrical laser fields positrons undergo
in the skin layer of overdense plasma, where the radiative spin-flip and
radiation reaction play significant roles. The positron polarization is robust
and could generally appear in future 100-PW-class laser-solid experiments for
various applications.
  A new source of highly polarized positrons, e.g., for a future polarized
muon collider, could be developed from laser-solid interactions by controlling
the positron polarization degree, yield, energy, and angular distribution, by
varying initial parameters such as laser intensity, polarization, wavelength,
and pulse duration as well as foil thickness, surface charge density, and
preplasma scale length. We propose several possible positron generators for
future experimental designs.
  The positron polarization in laser-solid interactions is also of theoretical
interest. Recent models possess challenges in self-consistently describing
the positron yield and polarization because the positrons are born in the
nonstationary, highly turbulent, and strongly field-driven plasma, which is
hard to be modeled by current one-dimensional or two-dimensional models. Future
seven-dimensional QED particle-in-cell simulations may have potential for
addressing this problem and further deepen our understanding of the complex
process of dense matter-field-laser interactions.
  The required positron yield for most proposed polarized positron sources is
order of magnitude larger than what the current laser-solid interactions can
provide.

OS temperature sensor for
densely-distributed thermal monitoring in systems on chip supporting dynamic
voltage and frequency scaling. The sensor front-end exploits a sub-threshold
PMOS-based circuit to convert the local temperature into two biasing currents.
These are then used to define two oscillation frequencies, whose ratio is
proportional to absolute-temperature. Finally, the sensor back-end translates
such frequency ratio into the digital temperature code. Thanks to its
low-complexity architecture, the proposed design achieves a very compact
footprint along with low-power consumption and high accuracy in a wide
temperature range. Moreover, thanks to a simple embedded line regulation
mechanism, our sensor supports voltage-scalability. The design was prototyped
in a 180nm CMOS technology with a 0{\deg}C $-$ 100{\deg}C temperature detection
range, a very wide supply voltage operating range from 0.6V up to 1.8V and very
small silicon area occupation of just 0.021$mm^2$. Experimental measurements
performed on 20 test chips have shown very competitive figures of merit,
including a resolution of 0.24{\deg}C, an inaccuracy of $\pm$1.4{\deg}C, a
sampling rate of about 1.5kHz and an energy per conversion of 1.06nJ at
standard voltage ($V_{DD}=1.8V$ and $V_{THN}=0.8V$). To the best of the
authors' knowledge, the proposed sensor achieves the highest temperature
resolution for a fully-digital IC, along with the lowest energy per conversion
in the sub-mW category and the lowest silicon area occupation for a
temperature range of 100{\deg}C.

continuum cores in the Dragon infrared dark cloud (also
known as G28.37+0.07 or G28.34+0.06) is analyzed statistically. Based on their
association with molecular outflows, the sample is divided into protostellar
and starless cores. Statistical tests suggest that the protostellar cores are
more massive than the starless cores, even after temperature and opacity biases
are accounted for. We suggest that the mass difference indicates core mass
growth since their formation. The mass growth implies that massive star
formation may not be initiated by the collapse of massive prestellar cores,
but rather by the continued accretion of smaller cores until they reach the
threshold for the collapse. Due to the limited number of cores in the present
sample, we do not want to conclude that this is the only scenario for massive
star formation. Further 1.3 mm or higher-resolution observations at longer
wavelengths are necessary to investigate the mass growth and associated star
formation dynamics systematically.
  We find that the protostellar cores are physically associated with 22 GHz
H2O masers, while no maser emission is found in the starless cores. This
suggests that the appearance of 22 GHz H2O masers is an early or critical phase
in the evolution of the cores in Dragon infrared dark cloud. The association
of the masers with the protostellar cores leads to an average maser lifetime
of less than 20,000 years. This, combined with a typical maser luminosity,
results in a total H2O maser gas mass of approximately 0.01-0.03 M$_{\odot}$
associated with the 1.3 mm cores in Dragon infrared dark cloud. Further
observations are necessary to constrain the role of H2O masers in massive
star formation.
  Five 22 GHz H2O maser sources are found to be associated with SiO outflow
sources. Three of them are protostellar cores without clear sign of interaction
with their surrounding gas. The strong H2O maser emission suggests that they
may be an interaction-mediated protostellar evolution stage, and the stage is
more frequent or more efficient for massive star formation. The other two are
already in an later interaction stage, interacting with their surrounding gas
at different extent. This suggests that the interaction-mediated protostellar
evolution stage is not a unique path to massive star formation.

  We present a numerical scheme based on Generalized Likelihood Uncertainty
Estimation (GLUE) for predicting the life-time of autonomous underwater
vessels (AUVs). The lifetime prediction is important for search and rescue
operations, and also for coordination of multiple AUVs. The proposed scheme
uses (1) nonlinear modeling of an AUV in a circular path to represent the
motion of the vehicle, (2) a switch based model to represent the state of the
battery and (3) a Bayesian framework to model the uncertainty in the state and
predict the lifetime. We use the transition probabilities based on the
nonlinear model and the states of the switch to represent the transition
probability matrix of the discounted state transition model for applying the
GLUE algorithm. We validate the effectiveness of the scheme by analyzing the
convergence properties and also by numerical simulations.

used by states and language testing agencies alike to evaluate millions of
candidates for life-changing decisions ranging from college applications to

interpret the black-box nature of deep-learning based scoring algorithms.
Previous studies indicate that scoring models can be easily fooled. In this
paper, we explore the reason behind their surprising adversarial brittleness.
We utilize recent advances in interpretability to find the extent to which
features such as coherence, content, vocabulary, and relevance are important
for automated scoring mechanisms. We use this to investigate the
oversensitivity i.e., large change in output score with a little change in
input essay content) and overstability i.e., little change in output scores
with large changes in input essay content) of AES. Our results indicate that
autoscoring models, despite getting trained as "end-to-end" models with rich
contextual embeddings such as BERT, behave like bag-of-words models. A few
words determine the essay score without the requirement of any context making
the model largely overstable. This is in stark contrast to recent probing
studies on pre-trained representation learning models, which show that rich
linguistic features such as parts-of-speech and morphology are encoded by them.
Further, we also find that the models have learnt dataset biases, making them
oversensitive. To get either overstable or oversensitive behavior, the model
needs to be trained with explicit input features including explicit parts-of
speech tags, which seems to be missing in the case of AES. This is a
methodological insight that can be used to make the current score models more
interpretable and also potentially train models which are both efficient and
accurate.

  This article describes our type-based static verification tool HELMHOLTZ for
Michelson, which is a statically typed stack-based language for writing smart
contracts that are executed on the blockchain platform Tezos. HELMHOLTZ is
designed on top of our extension of Michelson's type system with refinement
types. HELMHOLTZ takes a Michelson program annotated with a user-defined
specification written in the form of a refinement type as input; it then
typechecks the program against the specification based on the refinement type
system, discharging the generated verification conditions with the SMT solver
Z3. We briefly introduce our refinement type system for the core calculus
Mini-Michelson of Michelson, which incorporates the characteristic features
such as compound datatypes (e.g., lists and pairs), higher-order functions, and
invocation of another contract. \HELMHOLTZ{} successfully verifies several
practical Michelson programs, including one that transfers money to an account
and that checks a digital signature.

update/time-efficient operations (e.g., insertion of a single point) are
geometric and intuitive to comprehend. The algorithm can also be seen as an

CT denoising thanks to its superior performance despite the fast computational
time. In particular, cycleGAN has been demonstrated as a powerful unsupervised
learning scheme to improve the low-dose CT image quality without requiring
matched high-dose reference data. Unfortunately, one of the main limitations of
the cycleGAN approach is that it requires two deep neural network generators at
the training phase, although only one of them is used at the inference phase.
The secondary auxiliary generator is needed to enforce the cycle-consistency,
but the additional memory requirement and increases of the learnable parameters
are the main huddles for cycleGAN training. To address this issue, here we
propose a novel cycleGAN architecture using a single switchable generator. In
particular, a single generator is implemented using adaptive instance
normalization (AdaIN) layers so that the baseline generator converting a
low-dose CT image to a routine-dose CT image can be switched to a generator
converting high-dose to low-dose by simply changing the AdaIN code. Thanks to
the shared baseline network, the additional memory requirement and weight
increases are minimized, and the training can be done more stably even with
small training data. Experimental results show that the proposed method
outperforms the previous cycleGAN approaches while using only about half the
parameters.

remarkable success in dialog understanding tasks. However, current contrastive
learning solely considers the self-augmented dialog samples as positive samples
and treats all other dialog samples as negative ones, which enforces dissimilar
representations even for dialogs that are semantically related. In this paper,
we propose SPACE-2, a tree-structured pre-trained conversation model, which
learns dialog representations from limited labeled dialogs and large-scale
unlabeled dialog corpora via semi-supervised contrastive pre-training.
Concretely, we first define a general semantic tree structure (STS) to unify
the inconsistent annotation schema across different dialog datasets, so that
the rich structural information stored in all labeled data can be exploited.
Then we propose a novel multi-view score function to increase the relevance of
all possible dialogs that share similar STSs and only push away other
completely different dialogs during supervised contrastive pre-training. To
fully exploit unlabeled dialogs, a basic self-supervised contrastive loss is
also added to refine the learned representations. Experiments show that our
method can achieve new state-of-the-art results on the DialoGLUE benchmark
consisting of seven datasets and four popular dialog understanding tasks. For
reproducibility, we release the code and data at

propagation with feature alignment to effectively exploit information from the
entire input video. In this study, we redesign BasicVSR by proposing
second-order grid propagation and flow-guided deformable alignment. We show
that by empowering the recurrent framework with the enhanced propagation and
alignment, one can exploit spatiotemporal information across misaligned video

be used as a plugin in a cascaded framework to achieve even better
performance. In addition to the basic framework, we also revisit the loop
structure in video super-resolution and propose a simple but effective loop
method called LoopVSR. LoopVSR uses a loop framework to learn a recurrent

input video and the intermediate feature maps in each loop. Experimental
results show that our methods can be coupled to achieve state-of-the-art

from training on multiple related tasks by exploiting similarities among them.
At the same time, the trained agent is able to solve a wider range of different
problems. While this effect is well documented for model-free multi-task
methods, we demonstrate a detrimental effect when using a single learned
dynamics model for multiple tasks. Thus, we address the fundamental question of
whether model-based multi-task reinforcement learning benefits from shared
dynamics models in a similar way model-free methods do from shared policy
networks. Using a single dynamics model, we see clear evidence of task
confusion and reduced performance. As a remedy, enforcing an internal structure
for the learned dynamics model by training isolated sub-networks for each task
notably improves performance while using the same amount of parameters. We
illustrate our findings by comparing both methods on a simple gridworld and a
more complex vizdoom multi-task experiment.
  Our results indicate that a dedicated dynamics model is not automatically
beneficial for multi-task reinforcement learning. We argue that this is because
a generic model does not exploit similarities among related tasks as effectively
as a shared policy network does. To make model-based multi-task learning more
effective, we suggest dedicating isolated models (or layers) to each task.
Perhaps not surprisingly, this mirrors common practice in model-free multi-task
methods, which use a separate policy network for each task.

propose a regularized conditional Wasserstein GAN that can generate dozens of
high-quality posterior samples per second. Using quantitative evaluation
metrics like conditional Fr\'{e}chet inception distance, we demonstrate that

the THz communication is conventionally envisioned for short-range wireless
applications due to the high atmospheric absorption at THz frequencies,
multi-hop directional transmissions can be enabled to extend the communication
range. However, to realize multi-hop THz communications, conventional beam
training schemes, such as exhaustive search or hierarchical methods with a
fixed number of training levels, can lead to a very large time overhead. To
address this challenge, in this paper, a novel hierarchical beam training
scheme with dynamic training levels is proposed to optimize the performance of
multi-hop THz links. In fact, an optimization problem is formulated to maximize
the overall spectral efficiency of the multi-hop THz link by dynamically and
jointly selecting the number of beam training levels across all the constituent
single-hop links. To solve the problem in presence of unknown channel state
information, noise, and path loss, a new reinforcement learning solution based
on the multi-armed bandit (MAB) is developed. Simulation results show the fast
convergence of the proposed scheme in presence of random channels and noise.
The results also show that the proposed scheme can yield up to 75% performance
gain, in terms of spectral efficiency, compared to the conventional
hierarchical beam training with a fixed number of training levels.
Moreover, the results show that the proposed scheme can reduce the beam training
time by up to 50% compared to the conventional exhaustive search beam training
scheme.

Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) is proposed to improve the limited pitch
controllability of vanilla WaveNet (WN) using pitch-dependent dilated
convolution neural networks (PDCNNs). Specifically, as a probabilistic
autoregressive generation model with stacked dilated convolution layers, WN
achieves high-fidelity audio waveform generation. However, the pure-data-driven
nature and the lack of prior knowledge of audio signals degrade the pitch
controllability of WN. For instance, it is difficult for WN to precisely
generate the periodic components of audio signals when the given auxiliary
fundamental frequency ($F_{0}$) features are outside the $F_{0}$ range observed
in the training data. To address this problem, QPNet with two novel designs is
proposed. First, the PDCNN component is applied to dynamically change the
network architecture of WN according to the given auxiliary $F_{0}$ features.
Second, a cascaded network structure is utilized to simultaneously model the
long- and short-term dependencies of quasi-periodic signals such as speech. The
performances of single-tone sinusoid and speech generations are evaluated. The
experimental results show the effectiveness of the PDCNNs for unseen auxiliary
$F_{0}$ features and the effectiveness of the cascaded structure for speech
generation.

remotely and concurrently. We describe the motivation, design and
implementation of this interface; and we present details from a user study
working with this system.

clitics, part-of-speech, lemma, gloss, and dialect for the ISODIAC corpus.

useful for semantic search and they can also help in semantic disambiguation.

into a single subword) may lead to data drift when training semantic models on
annotated data. Thus, using glosses with annotated data can help to
guarantee consistency of the data across different systems.

impulsivity further leads to an interesting discussion on the evolution of a
population and how it may be characterized by the Tsallis distribution. In

variance will lead to an univariate scenario of the Tsallis distribution. We
also show that an increase in the variance of impulsivity with a fixed mean

the existence of two distinct agent groups in a system. These findings further
lead to a discussion on the effect of the fluctuation of impulsivity on the

system consisting of agents with an average mean impulsivity. This may be
